## Abstract

We present a search for polarization oscillation of the Crab Nebula, also known as Tau A, at millimeter wavelengths using observations with the Simons Array, the successor experiment to Polarbear. We follow up on previous work by Polarbear using 90 GHz band data of the 2023 observing season of the Simons Array to evaluate the variability of Tau A’s polarization angle. Tau A is widely used as a polarization angle calibration source in millimeter-wave astronomy, and thus it is necessary to validate the stability. Additionally, an interesting application of the time-resolved polarimetry of Tau A is to search for axion-like particles (ALPs). We do not detect a global signal across the frequencies considered in this analysis and place a median 95% upper bound of polarization oscillation amplitude $A<0.12^{\circ}$ over oscillation frequencies from 3.39 year-1 to 1.50 day-1. This constrains the ALP-photon coupling at a median 95% upper bound of $g_{a\gamma\gamma}<3.84\times 10^{-12}\times\left(m_{a}/10^{-21}\,\mathrm{eV}\right)$ in the mass range from $4.4\times 10^{-22}$ to $7.2\times 10^{-20}$ eV, assuming the ALP constitutes all of dark matter, its field is a stochastic Gaussian field, and it is the sole source of Tau A’s polarization angle oscillation. Additionally, we do not detect signal at the frequencies where 2.5 $\sigma$ hints were previously reported by Polarbear, but we do not exclude these signals at the 95% confidence level.

## I Introduction

Tau A, also known as the Crab Nebula, is a supernova remnant whose polarization emission is widely used as a polarization angle calibration source in millimeter-wave astronomy [1, 2]. The Polarbear collaboration recently demonstrated a method of investigating the time-varying polarization angle of Tau A using its 150 GHz band observations and reported a 2.5 $\sigma$ hint of polarization oscillation at 1/61 day-1 and 1/52 day-1 [[3], hereafter 3]. This potential variation is crucial for understanding the internal dynamics of Tau A and may be treated as a systematic error when using Tau A as a calibration source. Here we extend the results by applying the method to data from independent observations at 90 GHz with Polarbear-2a (PB-2a), the first receiver of the successor experiment of Polarbear, the Simons Array.

In addition to probing the stability of Tau A as a millimeter-wave calibration source, 3 explored its applications to the search for axion-like particles (ALPs), assuming the observed time-varying polarization angle is induced by electromagnetic coupling to ALPs. The reported hint of signal is inconsistent with other studies searching for ALP-induced oscillations in the same mass range [4, 5, 6, 7], highlighting the need for this paper to apply 3’s method as a consistency check. Originally proposed to solve the strong CP problem [8, 9, 10, 11], the QCD axion and its generic pseudoscalar form, the ALP, are prime particle candidates of dark matter and are therefore of broad astrophysical interest. The ALP does not solve the strong CP problem and is motivated by string theories [8, 12, 13]. Without a fixed relationship between its mass and the Standard Model, the ALP mass is theoretically unconstrained over a broad range [14, 15]. For masses around 10-22 eV, ALP dark matter resolves existing small-scale tensions in the standard cold dark matter model and fits the observed phenomenology of dark matter [16, 17].

In this paper, we exploit the ALP’s coupling to electromagnetism through the Chern-Simons term, introducing a birefringence of the ALP field [18, 19] and rotating the polarization angle of the photon propagating through the ALP field as

$$ \psi=\frac{g_{a\gamma\gamma}}{2}(\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}-\phi_{\mathrm{emit}}) $$

where $g_{a\gamma\gamma}$ is the ALP-photon coupling, $\phi_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is the ALP field where the photon is observed, and $\phi_{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the ALP field where the photon was emitted. We consider the case in which the ALP behaves as wave-like dark matter, for which the time variation of its field is described by a single mode sinusoid with period $h/(m_{a}c^{2})$ where $m_{a}$ is the ALP mass. For the mass range investigated in this study, $4.4\times 10^{-22}$ to $7.2\times 10^{-20}$ eV, the ALP’s coherence length is much shorter than the distance to Tau A [20] and the ALP Compton wavelength is much smaller than the size of Tau A [21]. Thus, as in 3, the ALP-induced polarization oscillation of Tau A can be modeled as

$$ \psi(t)=\psi_{0}+\frac{g_{a\gamma\gamma}\phi_{0}}{2}\sin\left(\frac{m_{a}c^{2}}{\hbar}t+\theta\right), $$

where $\psi_{0}$ is the polarization angle of Tau A.

In addition to studying the polarization angle variability of Tau A as a polarization angle calibrator at 90 GHz to extend Polarbear’s study at 150 GHz, using the 90 GHz band data of PB-2a to study axion-like polarization angle oscillations enables a check against frequency-dependent systematics such as Faraday rotations to Polarbear’s 150 GHz ALP search. This investigation into the PB24 ALP search is feasible because the ALP signal coherence time is greater than 100 years for the mass range of interest of this paper and thus remains coherent across Polarbear’s observations from 2016–2017 and PB-2a from 2023. To follow up on the results of the previous publication, the analysis method is purposely kept as identical as possible.

This paper is organized as follows: In Sec. II, we provide an overview of the instrument and its polarization modulator. In Sec III, we describe the Tau A observations used in this analysis. In Sec. IV, we describe the analysis method used in this paper, closely adapted from 3, and in Sec. V, the framework used to check for internal consistency against spurious results. In Sec. VI, we present the results of the analysis in Tau A polarization angle oscillation and limits on the ALP-photon coupling constant. We close in Sec. VII with concluding remarks and expectations of a follow-up study by the Simons Array.

## II Instrument Overview

### II.1 Site, telescope and receiver

The Simons Array is a millimeter-wave observatory on Cerro Toco in the Atacama Desert of Chile at an elevation of 5,200 m [22]. It upgrades and expands the Polarbear instrument into an array consisting of two dichroic polarimeters: Polarbear-2a (PB-2a) and PB-2b. Each telescope consists of a 2.5 m primary reflector arranged in an off-axis Gregorian-Dragone configuration that satisfies the Mizuguchi-Dragone condition, minimizing cross-polarization systematics and aberrations [23, 24, 25, 26]. The observation bands of PB-2a are centered at 90 and 150 GHz, with beams of 5.2 and 3.5 arcmin FWHM, respectively [27, 28]. The telescope houses a receiver cryostat (see Fig. 1) containing a 500 mm Zotefoam vacuum window, three alumina re-imaging lenses at 4 K, a Lyot stop at 4 K, and a 365 mm focal plane at 0.3 K with more than 7,600 transition-edge sensor detectors. A hemispherical lenslet focuses the output of the re-imaging lenses onto a detector pixel on the focal plane [29]. Each pixel utilizes a broadband sinuous antenna to couple optical signals of two orthogonal polarization states into a microstrip circuit. The circuit separates the signals into the two PB-2a frequency bands using band-pass filters, which then route the signals to the detectors, yielding four detectors per pixel.

### II.2 Half-wave plate

PB-2a utilizes a continuously rotating half-wave plate (HWP) as a polarization modulator, rotating at 2 Hz and placed immediately in front of the receiver window at ambient temperature [30]. The HWP up-converts the incident polarization signal above $1/f$ unpolarized fluctuations, thereby suppressing low-frequency noise. Given Stokes parameters I, Q, and U, the raw time-ordered data (TOD) of a detector is modeled as

$$ \displaystyle d_{m}(t)=I(t)+\varepsilon\mathrm{Re}\left\{\left[Q(t)+iU(t)\right]e^{-i\left(4\chi\left(t\right)+2\theta_{\mathrm{det}}\right)}\right\} \displaystyle+A\left(\chi,t\right)+\mathcal{N}_{m}, $$

where $\varepsilon$ is the polarization efficiency, $\chi\left(t\right)$ is the HWP rotation angle, $\theta_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the angle of the detector in telescope coordinates, $A\left(\chi,t\right)$ is the HWP synchronous signal, and $\mathcal{N}_{m}$ is the white noise of the detector. Note that polarization is modulated at four times the HWP frequency as captured in the modulation function, $e^{-i4\chi\left(t\right)}$ . The HWP synchronous signal is generated by many mechanisms related to instrumental polarization and non-idealities of the HWP. In a simplified model, the HWP synchronous signal is described by

$$ \displaystyle A\left(\chi,t\right)=\sum_{n=1}\mathrm{Re}\left\{A_{n}(t)e^{-in\chi(t)}\right\}, $$

where $A_{n}$ is the slowly-varying amplitude of the $n$ th harmonic. Throughout this paper, we refer to the 2nd and 4th harmonics of the HWP synchronous signal as the 2f and 4f signals, respectively. While an estimate of the HWP synchronous signal is subtracted from the TODs in the filtering process, it is also a crucial tool in the calibration process as discussed in Section IV.2.

## III Dataset

### III.1 Observations

In the observing season from September to December 2023, PB-2a observed Tau A on a near-daily schedule, with 4 separate observations each day. While both 90 and 150 GHz data are available from these observations, the focus of this analysis is placed on the 90 GHz dataset, and we leave the larger dataset to be analyzed for a future publication. Given that the PB-2a 90 GHz beam with $5.2^{\prime}$ FWHM is larger than the Tau A angular size of $7^{\prime}\times 5^{\prime}$ [31], the internal structure of Tau A is not resolved, but rather averaged during the calculation of the Tau A polarization angle (Sec IV.3).

Tau A is observed using a raster scan pattern, with the telescope continuously tracking Tau A in elevation while scanning back-and-forth in azimuth within 8∘ at 0.4∘/s. Between scans in azimuth, the elevation is stepped to ensure the entire focal plane observes Tau A. In contrast with 3 which only observed Tau A as it set from 39∘ to 30∘ in elevation, PB-2a observed Tau A for the entirety of its visibility as it rose and set between 30∘ and 45∘. Throughout a day of observations, it observed Tau A in 4 different scan-types of different elevation: rising (30∘ – 37∘), middle 1 (37∘ – 45∘), middle 2 (45∘ – 37∘), and setting (37∘ – 30∘). ## IV Analysis Method

### IV.1 TOD processing and demodulation

The first step in extracting the intensity and polarization signals from the raw TODs is to subtract the HWP synchronous signal. We reconstruct the angle of the HWP using data from an optical encoder, which we then downsample to the timestamps of our detector TODs. For the first eight harmonics of the HWP rotation frequency, we bandpass filter the TOD at the harmonic with a bandwidth of 0.2 Hz and demodulate the TOD with respect to that harmonic. The result is a template for the time-varying amplitude of the harmonic, which we subtract from the TOD. After subtracting the HWP synchronous signal, the polarization signal can be demodulated and extracted by multiplying $d_{m}\left(t\right)$ by twice the conjugate of the modulation function, $2e^{i4\chi\left(t\right)}$ , and low-pass filtering. To extract the intensity signal, we low-pass filter $d_{m}\left(t\right)$ after subtracting the HWP synchronous signal. In both cases, the low-pass filter has a cutoff frequency of 3.8 Hz.

There is leakage of the intensity signal into the polarization signal (I2P) due to detector non-linearity and instrumental polarization [32]. We use the extracted signals to estimate and remove this leakage using a principal component analysis (PCA), following the approach utilized in [33]. We compute the covariance matrices between the $I$ and $Q(U)$ TODs during the entire observation while masking out the regions where the telescope is not scanning with constant velocity and where the detector pointing is within a $12^{\prime}$ radius centered on Tau A. Assuming the intensity signal is dominated by unpolarized low-frequency atmospheric fluctuations, we perform PCA on these covariance matrices in order to estimate the leakage coefficients following [32]. After subtracting the estimated leakage, we fit the timestream of each constant-velocity subscan with a first-order polynomial and subtract it. When fitting the polynomial, we mask out sections of the TOD when the detector pointing is within a $12^{\prime}$ radius centered around Tau A.

We note that this method of leakage estimation differs from that used in 3 as we estimate leakage coefficients for each detector on an observation-by-observation basis rather than using fixed leakage coefficients for each detector. We will refer to the observation-by-observation leakage estimation method as the variable leakage model, and the method used in 3 as the fixed leakage model. We adopted the variable leakage model through iterative data validation tests. Both the fixed and variable leakage models passed the data validation tests, but the fixed leakage model required excluding five additional observations. These five observations have statistically significant variation exclusively in the I2U leakage. This variation does not correlate with any studied observing or instrumental conditions, such as the precipitable water vapor (PWV) or the bias conditions of our detectors. We concluded that the variable leakage model does not lead to a systematic misestimation of leakage and captures this variation well. Further discussion of possible systematic uncertainties due to this leakage estimation model is in Sec. V.3.2.

### IV.2 Calibration

#### IV.2.1 Relative Detector Gains

We use multiple observations of Jupiter to calibrate a chopped thermal source located behind the secondary mirror [34]. This thermal source is then used to calibrate the amplitude of the 2f component of the HWP synchronous signal in units of $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{CMB}}$ . We use the 2f signal because it is the brightest HWP synchronous signal harmonic. We expect that the 2f signal exists due to differential transmission and absorption between the crystal axes in the HWP [35], and so the amplitude of the 2f signal varies linearly with the brightness of the atmosphere. We fit a linear model between the 2f amplitude in $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{CMB}}$ and our proxy for atmospheric brightness, $\mathrm{PWV}/\sin\left(\mathrm{elevation}\right)$ , for each detector. We use this model to estimate the expected 2f brightness for a given observation, which is then used for gain calibration. We note here that because this analysis is focused on estimating the polarization angle of Tau A, we do not apply an overall gain calibration to our instrument coadded data that accounts for effects such as imperfect polarization efficiency in the PB-2a instrument.

#### IV.2.2 Time Constants

The time constants of our detectors cause an apparent phase lag between the reconstructed angle of the HWP and the detector TOD, appearing as an error in the polarization angle, which must be calibrated. Assuming that any measured variation in the phase of the 2f signal is due to the effect of the time constants and a single pole transfer function for the time constants, the phase rotation at 2f is not identical to the phase rotation at 4f, where the Tau A polarization signal lives. For each detector, we measure:

$$ \delta\psi^{2f(4f)}_{t,j}=\mathrm{average}_{j}\left(\psi^{2f(4f)}_{t,j}\right)-\psi_{t,j}^{2f(4f)} $$

where $\psi^{2f(4f)}$ is the phase of the 2f(4f) signal, $t$ is the index of the observation, $j$ is the index of the detector, and $\mathrm{average}_{j}(...)$ is an average over all observations. We fit a linear relationship between $\delta\psi_{t,j}^{2f}$ and $\delta\psi_{t,j}^{4f}$ as $\delta\psi^{4f}_{t,j}=C^{\tau}_{j}\delta\psi^{2f}_{t,j}$ and use this model to rotate the polarization basis at 4f using the measured variation in 2f phase for a given observation and detector:

$$ Q_{t,j}^{\prime}+iU_{t,j}^{\prime}=\left(Q_{t,j}+iU_{t,j}\right)\exp\left(-iC_{j}^{\tau}\delta\psi_{t,j}^{2f}\right). $$

Here, $Q_{t,j}$ and $U_{t,j}$ are the TODs for the Stokes parameters after the demodulation procedure described in Sec. IV.1. We note that a unique $C^{\tau}_{j}$ is fit for each individual detector in our analysis, as we expect this factor to vary based on the mean time constant of a given detector.

#### IV.2.3 Pointing

We calibrate the pointing for each detector for each observation using the Tau A intensity signal. For each detector in a given observation, we fit the measured intensity signal to an elliptical Gaussian model in equatorial coordinates. The offsets from the centers of the Gaussian fits to the expected Tau A position are then applied to the detector pointing. We discuss possible errors associated with our pointing reconstruction in Sec. V.3.3.

#### IV.2.4 Detector polarization angles

We use the full season of Tau A observations to calibrate the polarization angles of our detectors. Nominally, this means constructing season co-added maps of Tau A for each detector, $j$ , and rotating $Q_{t,j}+iU_{t,j}$ for each observation, $t$ , by the offset between the measured Tau A polarization angle in the co-added maps for each detector and the Tau A polarization angle as measured by IRAM [1].

When applying the polarization angle calibration for the entire season of data, a systematic correlation between the azimuth and elevation of an observation and the extracted Tau A polarization angle was discovered. In order to prevent any systematic contamination, we instead calibrate the polarization angles independently for the four distinct observation types described in Sec. III.1. Therefore, instead of constructing co-added maps over the course of the entire observing season, we construct co-added maps for each observation type and apply the polarization angle calibrations independently. This leads to a loss of sensitivity for some modes, and we simulate this effect in our transfer function, which we show in Fig. 3.

#### IV.2.5 Relative polarization angles between observations

In order to avoid systematic misestimation of the measured polarization angle between observations, we make use of the HWP synchronous signal. We assume that the 4f signal is dominated by optical systematics [32] and that the phase of this signal remains constant in instrumental coordinates between observations. We first attempt to correct for the phase lag due to the detector time constants as in Sec. IV.2.2. The 4f phase variation for an individual detector for a given observation after this correction is

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\delta\psi}^{4f}_{t,j} \displaystyle=\delta\psi_{t,j}^{4f}-C^{\tau}_{j}\delta\psi_{t,j}^{2f}. $$

We expect that any systematic rotations common to measured polarization angles in the focal plane, such as a misestimation of the HWP angle or a timing offset, will shift the distribution of $\tilde{\delta{\psi}}_{t,j}^{4f}$ away from $0$ . We estimate this systematic rotation as the median of the 4f variation over all detectors

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{t} \displaystyle\equiv\mathrm{median}_{j}\left(\tilde{\delta\psi}^{4f}_{t,j}\right), $$

and correct for this offset by rotating the polarization basis of our timestreams as

$$ Q^{\prime\prime}_{t,j}+iU^{\prime\prime}_{t,j}=\left(Q^{\prime}_{t,j}+iU^{\prime}_{t,j}\right)\exp\left(-i\alpha_{t}\right). $$

### IV.3 Angle measurement and statistical uncertainty

Our mapmaking pipeline projects the filtered and calibrated TODs onto flat sky maps with pixel widths of $2.4^{\prime}$ using a cylindrical equal-area projection. We estimate the polarization angle of Tau A in map-space following the method outlined in 3

$$ d_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\textrm{tan}^{-1}\left(\frac{\sum_{p}^{\diameter<16^{\prime}}U_{p}^{\textrm{Tau\ A}}}{\sum_{p}^{\diameter<16^{\prime}}Q_{p}^{\textrm{Tau\ A}}}\right) $$

where $d_{t}$ is the measured polarization angle for observation $t$ , $Q_{p}$ and $U_{p}$ are the $p$ -th $Q$ and $U$ map pixel in the observation co-added map. We show the co-added map of all observations in this analysis in Fig. 2 and highlight the integration area used to estimate the polarization angle. We note that we have increased the diameter of the integration area to $16^{\prime}$ to account for the increased beam size in the PB-2a experiment ( $5.2^{\prime}$ ) compared to the Polarbear experiment ( $3.6^{\prime}$ ). We also follow the bootstrap method outlined in 3 to generate white noise realizations and use these to estimate the statistical uncertainty on our polarization angle estimate, $\sigma_{t}$ . Our median statistical uncertainty in the polarization angle of Tau A is $0.25^{\circ}$ per observation.

### IV.4 Polarization oscillation spectrum estimation

For consistency, and to compare our results more directly with the 3 results, we choose to report on the same frequencies as the finer spaced frequencies in their analysis. The total length of the observing season considered in this analysis is shorter, so we cut out the lowest frequency modes to which we are insensitive. This leaves us with the following frequencies:

$$ f_{\mathrm{bins}}=\left\{\frac{45}{4860\Delta T},\frac{46}{4860\Delta T},...,\frac{2420}{4860\Delta T}\right\} $$

where $\Delta T$ corresponds to one sidereal day ( $\Delta T\approx 1-1/366.24\$ days). Our near-daily observing schedule means that power in frequencies below $1/2\Delta T$ is degenerate with frequencies between $1/2\Delta T$ and $3/2\Delta T$ due to aliasing. Through simulations, we confirmed that a signal with frequency between $1/2\Delta T$ and $3/2\Delta T$ will be measured at approximately 90% amplitude at the aliased frequency below $1/2\Delta T$ . Therefore, we extend the scientific results to

$$ f_{\mathrm{bins,result}}=\left\{\frac{N}{2\Delta T}+f_{\mathrm{bins}}\bigg|N=0,1,2\right\}. $$

We confirm that the data is internally consistent at the extended frequencies by scaling the systematic estimates and null statistics described in Sec. V by this aliasing factor and find that we still pass our data validation criteria.

We follow the exact procedure outlined in 3 to estimate the polarization oscillation amplitude at each of the frequencies. To summarize briefly, we perform least-squares spectral analysis (LSSA) on our timestream of Tau A polarization angles and their associated uncertainties. Similarly to 3, our estimate of the signal amplitude is biased, and we quantify this bias by estimating our transfer function, $F_{f}$ , in a manner identical to the procedure outlined in 3. The method for polarization angle calibration differs between the two analyses, which we take into account when calculating the transfer function for this analysis. The full transfer function can be seen in Fig. 3.

We use an identical test statistic as 3 to quantify the global significance for the preference of a signal:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\chi^{2}_{f} \displaystyle=\sum_{m,n\in\{\mathrm{real},\mathrm{imag}\}}\tilde{d}_{f}^{m}\tilde{N}_{mn}^{-1}\tilde{d}_{f}^{n} \displaystyle\Delta\chi^{2} \displaystyle=\textrm{max}_{f}\left(\Delta\chi^{2}_{f}\right), $$

where $d_{f}$ is the complex LSSA amplitude of the signal at frequency $f$ and $\tilde{N}_{mn}$ is our noise covariance matrix estimated using the same noise realizations we use to determine our statistical uncertainty. To follow up on the hint of signal seen in 3, we additionally use $\Delta\chi^{2}_{f}$ to test for the local significance of a signal at the two frequencies reported on in 3 (hereafter, the two PB24 frequencies): $1/61.4\ \textrm{day}^{-1},\ 1/52.1\ \textrm{day}^{-1}$ .

## V Data Validation

We utilize a blind analysis and only unblind the estimated polarization angles of Tau A and the associated oscillation spectrum after checking for internal consistency in our data using null tests. In this section, we will summarize the null tests and their results. We also report on the impact of potential sources of systematic error and utilize the weighted-correlation method to search for additional systematic contamination.

### V.1 Null test

In constructing the null tests for probing systematic errors across the entire frequency spectrum, we follow the analysis presented in 3. We split the data either based on a characteristic of an individual observation or on individual detectors and check for consistency between the two halves. Appendix A provides a brief description for each observation and detector split. Following 3, we calculate $\chi_{\mathrm{null}}^{\mathrm{DC}},\chi^{\mathrm{AC}}_{\mathrm{null}}$ and $\chi_{\mathrm{null}}^{2}$ . $\chi_{\mathrm{null}}^{\mathrm{DC}}$ represents the difference in the noise-weighted mean polarization angle between each half of the split; $\chi^{\mathrm{AC}}_{\mathrm{null}}$ and $\chi_{\mathrm{null}}^{2}$ capture the noise-weighted difference in the real/imaginary LSSA amplitudes in each half of the split. We use these statistics to compute six representative null statistics for both the observation-based and detector-based splits. We calculate the probability-to-exceed (PTE) for these representative null statistics by comparing to 1,440 bootstrap noise simulations. - 1. The PTE of the lowest PTE value11 1 As in 3, the PTE of the lowest (highest) PTE value is obtained by counting the number of simulations whose lowest (highest) PTE value is smaller (larger) than the observed lowest (highest) PTE value. is greater than 0.05.

- 2. The PTE of the highest PTE value is greater than 0.05.

Note that we require the pass criteria to be met for both the observation-based and detector-based null tests separately.

We also include null tests intended to probe for systematic errors at the two PB24 frequencies: $1/61.4$ day-1 and $1/51.2$ day-1. ### V.3 Systematic Errors

We follow many of the detailed systematic studies presented in 3. Here we will note any differences between the analyses and will summarize the results for the studies kept identical. In addition to the studies presented in the 3 analysis, we include a study for systematic polarization angle fluctuation due to our gain calibration. In Table 5, we show the RMS of the estimated systematic errors as well as the median statistical errors per observation.

#### V.3.1 Gain

A time-varying misestimation of the relative gain between detectors may propagate into an error on the polarization angle measurement of Tau A. In order to estimate this effect, we utilize a second calibration pipeline where we use each detector’s individual map of Tau A to calibrate its gain. We do this by fitting the Tau A signal in a detector’s intensity map to a two-dimensional Gaussian model and using the amplitude of this fit to calibrate the detector’s gain. We then estimate the systematic polarization angle fluctuation due to gain miscalibration as the difference in polarization angles between our nominal pipeline and this pipeline using Tau A for gain calibration. The systematic polarization angle fluctuation due to gain miscalibration is found to be 0.047∘ RMS.

#### V.3.2 Intensity to polarization leakage

As noted in Sec. IV.1, the I2P leakage in this analysis is estimated on an observation-by-observation basis. In order to estimate the systematic error due to I2P leakage misestimation, we take the difference of Tau A polarization angles from pipelines using variable I2P leakage estimation and fixed I2P leakage estimates. We only include observations that pass our null tests using both I2P leakage models. The RMS of the angle difference between the two pipelines is $0.09^{\circ}$ .

#### V.3.3 Pointing

Misestimation of the boresight pointing will result in incorrect conversions between the polarization angle in telescope coordinates and sky coordinates. We evaluate this uncertainty by considering the observation-by-observation variation in the celestial position of Tau A as observed by PB-2a. Because we calibrate the pointing for individual observations using the intensity signal of Tau A, we consider this to be representative of random statistical fluctuations in our calibration. We find the median polarization uncertainty due to pointing fluctuation to be $0.002^{\circ}$ .

#### V.3.4 Residual $1/f$

Correlated $1/f$ noise will be partially canceled during the bootstrap statistical uncertainty estimation process, and thus, isn’t fully represented in the statistical uncertainty estimates. We estimate the residual $1/f$ uncertainty as follows. For both bootstrap noise maps and Tau A maps, we estimate $\delta Q=\sum_{p}^{\mathrm{noise\,region}}Q_{p}$ and $\delta U=\sum_{p}^{\mathrm{noise\,region}}U_{p}$ for 96 independent noise regions with the same size as the one used to estimate $d_{t}$ but outside of the Tau A region. We estimate the uncertainty in the polarization angle, $\sigma_{t}$ , in the bootstrap maps and the Tau A maps using these noise samples. Assuming the noise regions of Tau A maps contain contributions from both statistical and residual $1/f$ noise whereas those of bootstrap maps contain contributions approximately from only statistical noise, we estimate the residual $1/f$ contribution by subtracting their variances following $\sigma_{1/f}=\sqrt{\sigma_{\mathrm{Tau\,A}}^{2}-\sigma_{\mathrm{bootstrap}}^{2}}$ . The polarization angle fluctuation is calculated to be 0.016∘ RMS.

#### V.3.5 Filtering and mapmaking bias

The filtering and mapmaking pipeline will bias estimates of the Tau A polarization angle. A variation in these biases over time will produce a systematic polarization angle fluctuation. We estimate this systematic fluctuation with simulations. We simulate the Tau A map by convolving the IRAM Tau A map with a Gaussian beam with a FWHM identical to PB-2a’s beam at 90 GHz. This serves as an input map as we simulate each detector’s TOD for each observation by scanning the map, modulating the signal using HWP angles, and applying the same analysis method used on PB-2a data to estimate its angle. The systematic polarization angle fluctuation is calculated to be 0.026∘ RMS.

A slightly different set of detectors is used for each observation in this analysis. We find the fluctuation of the Tau A polarization angle due to detector polarization angle miscalibration to be 0.03∘ RMS.

## VII Conclusion

We have used the 2023 season of Tau A observations from the PB-2a receiver to investigate the polarization variability of Tau A. We place a median 95% upper bound on polarization angle oscillation at $A<0.12^{\circ}$ for frequencies ranging from 3.39 year-1 to 1.50 day-1. To the best of our knowledge, this is the tightest bound placed on the polarization variability of Tau A at 90 GHz. Additionally, we investigate the hint of signal reported in 3. We detect no signal at either of the frequencies presented in the 3 analysis. However, we do not exclude the signals seen in 3 at the 95% confidence level. When converting the polarization oscillation constraints to ALP constraints, we find a median 95% upper bound on the ALP-photon coupling $g_{a\gamma\gamma}<\left(3.84\times 10^{-12}\right)\times\left(m_{a}/10^{-21}\,\mathrm{eV}\right)$ in the mass range from $4.4\times 10^{-22}$ to $7.2\times 10^{-20}$ eV.

The PB-2a telescope continued regular observations of Tau A through August 2024. We expect these observations to increase our data volume by a factor of $\approx$ 2 if the data selection efficiency remains consistent with that presented in this analysis. This would result in a sensitivity increase of $\approx$ 45%. With this sensitivity, we expect to test the 3 hint at the 95% level. In addition to observing at 90 GHz, PB-2a observes in a band centered at 150 GHz. Further analysis including this second observing band will provide a check for frequency-dependent systematics, as any ALP-induced oscillation will be frequency-independent.

## Appendix A Null test splits

This section describes the null test splits introduced in Sec. V. For the following detector splits, “A/B pixel handedness”, “Q/U type pixel”, “top/bottom detector”, “left/right on focal plane”, and “upper/lower on focal plane”, the data is split according to a discrete property of the detector, and thus, there won’t necessarily be exactly equal data volume in each half of the split. However, for the remaining detector and observation based splits, the data is separated at the median value of the split parameter.

The detector based splits are

- • “A/B pixel handedness”: the sinuous antennas on the focal plane contain two types of pixel handedness, referred to as A and B, that are mirror images of each other. We split the detectors based on their associated antennas’ handedness to check for systematics related to the polarization angle frequency dependence of the sinuous antenna.

- • “Q/U type pixel”: there are two sets of sinuous antenna polarization angles on the focal plane. We split the data between the types to check for problems in device fabrication.

- • “top/bottom detector”: there is a pair of detectors for each band associated with a single antenna. Each detector is sensitive to both orthogonal polarization states when utilizing the rotating HWP. We split the data along this property to test for device mismatch.

- • “left/right on focal plane” and “upper/lower on focal plane”: we split the data based on the physical location of the detector on the focal plane to check for optical systematics or systematics confined to specific detector wafers.

- • “gain”: we split the detectors based on the gain calibration factor to probe for problems associated with the calibration.

- • “I2P amp”: we split the data based on the estimated amplitude of the I2P leakage to probe for systematic contamination coupling through I2P leakage.

- • “4f amp/2f amp”: we split the data based on the amplitude of the 2nd and 4th harmonics of the HWP synchronous signal. This probes for systematics related to the amplitude of instrumental polarization or optical systematics observed by different detectors.

- • “4f phase/2f phase”: we split the data based on the phase of the 2nd and 4th harmonics of the HWP synchronous signal. This probes for issues related to the per-observation polarization angle calibration.

- • “white noise”: we split the data based on the white noise level of the detectors to probe for ineffective data selection or noise modeling.

The observation splits are

- • “1st/2nd half of season”: we split the observations chronologically into halves to probe for time-dependent miscalibrations or changes in the instrument.

- • “PWV”: we split the observations based on the PWV during the observation to probe loading or weather-dependent systematics.

- • “sun distance/moon distance”: we split the observations based on the angular distance to the sun/moon. This probes for potential optical systematics caused by far-sidelobe contamination.

- • “elevation”: we split the observations into high and low elevation observations to check for residual systematics associated with the observing orientation.

- • “4f phase/2f phase”: we split the observations based on the median HWP synchronous signal 2f/4f phases over all active detectors in the observation. This is sensitive to observations with residual systematic polarization angle miscalibrations.

- • “4f amp”: we split the observations based on the median amplitude of the HWP synchronous signal 4f amplitude over all active detectors in the observation. This probes for systematic differences in observations with varying instrumental polarization.

- • “white noise”: we split the observations based on the median white noise level over all active detectors in the observation. This is sensitive to observations with anomalous noise that may contaminate the polarization angle estimate.

- • “gain”: we split the observations based on the median gain over all active detectors in the observation. This is sensitive to systematic gain miscalibrations.

- • “I2P amplitude”: we split the observations based on the median I2P amplitude over all active detectors in the observation. This probes for systematic I2P leakage misestimation.

- • “HWP vacuum”: The HWP vacuum split refers to the pressure in the vacuum system used to adhere the anti-reflection coating on the birefringent sapphire optical surfaces. This vacuum level naturally degrades over time and is regularly pumped out during maintenance. We split the observations based on the vacuum level of the HWP system during the observation. This probes for potential systematics associated with HWP optical stack.

## Abstract

We have developed and demonstrated a method for measuring circular polarization at $90\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ by combining a quarter-wave plate (QWP) and a continuously rotating half-wave plate (HWP). While many bolometric experiments at millimeter wavelengths focus on measuring linear polarization, observations of circular polarization in millimeter waves may open a new window into astrophysics and cosmology. We present a novel approach to circular-polarization search using linear-polarization-sensitive detectors by incorporating a QWP in the optics. The Simons Array was originally designed for precise linear polarization measurements, and we subsequently installed a QWP in front of the receiver targeting $90\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ . The QWP converts incident circular polarization to linear polarization, allowing detection with our detectors. Laboratory measurements demonstrate a QWP conversion efficiency of 99.0%. We apply our method to observations of unpolarized and linearly polarized bright sources, Jupiter and Tau A. Using these observations, we establish the calibration and characterize the instrumental leakages relevant to circular polarization measurements. The measured polarization efficiency adopted for Stokes $V$ is $46\pm 2$ %, and the measured U-to-V leakage is $-11.7\pm 5.1$ %. We measure a circular polarization fraction of $V/I=0.78\pm 0.42$ % for Tau A, showing no significant detection and providing a consistency check of the calibration and systematic-uncertainty treatment. These results establish the instrument response model and calibration parameters used for the companion circular-polarization source search.

## 1 Introduction

Observations of millimeter-wave polarization provide rich information for understanding the universe. One of the main observation targets at millimeter waves is the cosmic microwave background (CMB) linear polarization. In particular, CMB $B$ -modes generated by primordial gravitational waves are expected to be a powerful probe of cosmic inflation at the beginning of the universe Seljak and Zaldarriaga (1997); Kamionkowski et al. (1997).

The CMB community is growing, including both ground- and space-based experiments. Current CMB observations mainly aim to push the constraint of the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ further or detect the $B$ -mode polarization induced by primordial gravitational waves. These CMB experiments utilize the technology of an incoherent detector, which directly measures the intensity of incident CMB signals. Thanks to their high sensitivity and low noise, Transition-Edge Sensor (TES) bolometers are often used Duff et al. (2016); Stevens et al. (2020). By increasing the number of bolometers deployed, these telescopes aim to achieve high sensitivity. For example, the Simons Array (SA) experiment, which is the successor of the Polarbear experiment Kermish et al. (2012); Kermish (2012); Collaboration (2020b); Collaboration (2020a) at the Atacama Desert in Chile, was designed to measure the CMB linear polarization with high accuracy Suzuki et al. (2016).

Though the mainstream of recent millimeter-wave polarization experiments focuses on linear polarization, observations of CMB circular polarization can probe a variety of effects Eimer et al. (2024); Mainini et al. (2013); Nagy et al. (2017); Padilla et al. (2020), such as galactic synchrotron emission Planck Collaboration (2020); Legg and Westfold (1968); King and Lubin (2016); Eimer et al. (2024), Faraday conversion by Population (Pop) III stars De and Tashiro (2015), scattering with the cosmic neutrino background Mohammadi (2014), photon-photon forward scattering Hoseinpour et al. (2020), and Lorentz violation Caloni et al. (2023). The search for circular polarization in astronomical sources may reveal magnetic field structures Huang and Shcherbakov (2011); Wiesemeyer et al. (2011); Ruszkowski and Begelman (2002). In addition, the Earth’s atmospheric emission is circularly polarized due to the Zeeman effect Lenoir (1968); Keating et al. (1998); Hanany and Rosenkranz (2003); Spinelli et al. (2011). The CLASS and Polarbear experiments detected this circular polarization Petroff et al. (2020); Fujino et al. (2025). CLASS uses a variable-delay polarization modulator, whereas Polarbear takes advantage of the nonidealities of a continuously rotating half-wave plate (HWP) Chuss et al. (2012); Harrington et al. (2018); Fujino et al. (2023); Nagy et al. (2017).

Among several methods to measure circular polarization in millimeter waves Petroff et al. (2020); Nagy et al. (2017); Eimer et al. (2024); Fujino et al. (2025), our approach is to use a quarter-wave plate (QWP) van Vliet and de Graauw (1981). The QWP gives a phase difference of $\lambda/4$ between the two linear components of the input signals. It converts circular polarization into linear polarization, allowing Stokes $V$ to be modulated by the HWP and measured with the existing receiver. We fabricated the QWP made of Rexolite 1422, cross-linked polystyrene.11 1 C-Lec Plastics, Inc., Philadelphia, PA, USA. We cut grooves into both sides of the plate, adjusting the thickness to optimize the QWP for a $90\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ circular polarization search.

The QWP was installed in the SA telescope that hosts the Polarbear-2b (PB-2b) receiver. PB-2b is the second receiver in the SA, which was designed to measure the linear polarization of the CMB Suzuki et al. (2016). It did not originally have circular polarization as a science goal. It contains 7588 TES bolometers and utilizes a cryogenic continuously rotating HWP for modulation of the incoming linear polarization signal Hill et al. (2020). The QWP is located on the sky side of the receiver and operates at ambient air temperature. By converting Stokes $V$ before HWP modulation, the QWP enables the existing system to measure circular polarization without a drastic change to the telescope structure or analysis pipeline.

The main goal of this analysis is to characterize the instrumental response and determine the calibration parameters relevant to circular polarization measurements, including those associated with nonidealities of the QWP and other instrumental components. Tau A, also known as the Crab Nebula, and Jupiter observations are used for characterization and calibration. They have high-intensity signals, and Tau A has large linear polarization of about 8.8% at our target frequency Aumont et al. (2010). Since the QWP converts the source circular polarization to linear polarization, the overall analysis pipeline is similar to those used for linear polarization analysis, such as that used in the analysis of Polarbear-2a (PB-2a) observations of Tau A Adkins et al. (2026). We developed the analysis methodology and the calibration method by utilizing the QWP, and we identified systematic errors unique to this type of measurement. We estimated the efficiency and leakages from Tau A and Jupiter observations. The analysis method described here is used for searching for circular polarization in astronomical sources, for which we apply blind analysis. The results are presented in a companion paper The POLARBEAR Collaboration () (hereafter Paper II).

This paper presents the development of the QWP and characterizes circular polarization search with the SA. Section 2 describes the method for the circular polarization search with the QWP and its evaluation at a lab. Section 3 presents the Tau A and Jupiter datasets. In section 4, we report the analysis from time-ordered data processing to map making. We discuss the results of on-sky characterization with Tau A and Jupiter observations in section 5. We conclude the paper in section 6.

### 2.2 Simons Array instrument

The SA is a ground-based experiment on the Atacama plateau in Chile that aims to measure polarization of millimeter-wave signals. PB-2a is the first receiver in the SA, while PB-2b is the second Suzuki et al. (2016); Siritanasak (2018); Lowry (2021); Ito (2022). The two receivers are very similar in their designs. The QWP discussed here is used with PB-2b.

The telescope employs an off-axis Gregorian optical design. The design of the reflective optics is identical to that of the Polarbear-1 (PB-1) telescope, the predecessor to SA Kermish et al. (2012). A cold Lyot stop in the receiver optics defines an effective primary aperture of $2.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ , projected along boresight onto the central, high-precision panel of the primary mirror. It satisfies the Mizuguchi-Dragone condition, in order to mitigate cross-polarization and astigmatism effects Tran (2003). The field of view is circular with 4.5-degree diameter Matsuda (2017); Lowry (2021), and an angular resolution is designed to be 5.2 (3.5) arc minutes full width at half maximum at 90 (150) GHz Tomaru and others (2012). The receiver is cooled by sorption refrigerators Bhatia and others (2000). Figure 2 shows the PB-2b receiver. It consists mainly of a $0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ diameter vacuum window, three lenses cooled to $4\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , and a $0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ focal plane. A cryogenic HWP is located between the vacuum window and the lenses Hill and others (2018). The QWP is installed $150\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ away from the window at ambient temperature. It is designed to cover all the light rays without intercepting the optical path between the primary and secondary mirrors.

*Figure 2: Cross section of the PB-2b receiver, with key elements labeled Ito (2022).*

The PB-2b design is almost the same as that of PB-2a Adkins et al. (2026). PB-2b, however, uses a cryogenic HWP that consists of three-stacked sapphire with two-layer anti-reflection (AR) coatings Hill et al. (2020); Sakaguri et al. (2024); Bixler et al. (2026). The HWP rotates at $2\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ and modulates linear polarization signals to mitigate atmospheric 1/f noise. It prevents systematics arising from different responses in pairs of polarimeters by rotating continuously Takakura et al. (2017); Kusaka and others (2014); Essinger-Hileman et al. (2016). The PB-2b HWP is operated at a cryogenic temperature of $50\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ to minimize the effects of thermal radiation. It is located near the telescope’s Gregorian focus. Its drive system consists of a superconducting magnetic bearing and a synchronous electromagnetic motor Hill et al. (2020).

The focal plane consists of dichroic detectors, with each spectral band (centered at 90 and $150\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ ) split into orthogonal linear polarizations. Each observing band has a fractional bandwidth of approximately 30%. The receiver is equipped with 7588 bolometers. These bolometers are on seven wafers on the focal plane, each containing 271 pixels. Each pixel features a lenslet-coupled sinuous antenna for orthogonal polarizations, which feeds two superconducting TES bolometers per frequency band. These TES bolometers have a transition temperature of about $450\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{K}$ Westbrook et al. (2018).

### 2.3 Quarter-wave plate

#### 2.3.1 Design and fabrication

There are two common ways to make a QWP van Vliet and de Graauw (1981), and the technique has been well-established. One approach is to fabricate the QWP from a birefringent material, which has different dielectric constants along two orthogonal directions Marrone and Rao (2008); Marrone (2006). The other approach is to artificially produce the anisotropy by making many grooves in a slab of isotropic material Rao et al. (1998); RAO (1999). We adopt the latter. Our QWP is made of Rexolite 1422, which is cross-linked polystyrene. It is a dielectric with low loss and high transmittance at millimeter-wavelength. The dielectric constant is 2.54 Lamb (1996). It is not a birefringent material, but it works as a QWP by cutting grooves (figure 3).

*Figure 3: QWP drawing and photo. Left: 3D CAD model of the QWP. Right: Photo of the QWP with mounting jigs.*

The Rexolite plate used in SA is $610\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ $\times$ $610\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ in size. It is determined to fit the existing telescope’s structure (see section 2.4 for more details). We set the rib and groove widths to be equal. Under this assumption, the refractive indices parallel (perpendicular) to the grooves, $n_{par}$ ( $n_{perp}$ ), are described as Kirschbaum and Chen (1957),

$$ \displaystyle n_{par}^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{\kappa_{1}+\kappa_{2}}{2} \displaystyle n_{perp}^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{2\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}}{\kappa_{1}+\kappa_{2}}, $$

where $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$ are the dielectric constants of the ribs and the grooves, respectively. This equal-width configuration approximately maximizes the difference between $n_{par}$ and $n_{perp}$ (figure 3). Because the Rexolite dielectric constant is 2.54 Lamb (1996), and the dielectric constant of the air is one, $\kappa_{2}=1$ , the design indices are $n_{par}=1.33$ and $n_{perp}=1.20$ . The groove depth is determined to produce a quarter wavelength difference in path length parallel and perpendicular to the grooves. The initial plate thickness before machining the grooves is about $15.6\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ . Our target frequency is $90\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ , and the calculated design groove depth is $3.18\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ . The groove width and the rib width are $0.635\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ . The grooves are cut into the Rexolite plate using a slitting saw on a computer-controlled milling machine. Note that we do not apply an AR coating to the QWP because Rexolite has a relatively low dielectric constant.

To characterize the QWP and express the polarization state, we utilize a Mueller matrix $M$ , which is a $4\times 4$ matrix operating as $\vec{S}_{\mathrm{out}}=M\vec{S}_{\mathrm{in}}$ . Here, $\vec{S}_{\mathrm{in}}$ ( $\vec{S}_{\mathrm{out}}$ ) is the input (output) Stokes vectors, $\vec{S}=(I,Q,U,V)^{T}$ . Our QWP can be modeled as

$$ M_{\mathrm{QWP}}=\begin{pmatrix}T&\rho&0&0\\
\rho&T&0&0\\
0&0&\epsilon&-\eta\\
0&0&\eta&\epsilon\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $T$ is the transmission, $\rho$ is the differential transmission between the two QWP axes, $\eta$ corresponds to the conversion efficiency, and $\epsilon$ represents the unconverted Stokes $U$ or $V$ component. In our circular polarization measurement, a nonzero $\epsilon$ appears as U-to-V leakage. An ideal QWP has $T=1$ , $\rho=0$ , $\eta=1$ , and $\epsilon=0$ .

#### 2.4.2 Polarization optics model

Figure 7 shows the polarization signal flow through the optical system and defines the Stokes-parameter notation used in this paper. The Stokes vectors $\vec{S}_{\textrm{sky}}$ , $\vec{S}_{\textrm{in}}$ , $\vec{S}_{\textrm{conv}}$ , and $\vec{S}_{\textrm{out}}$ denote $(I,Q,U,V)^{T}$ in sky coordinates, in telescope coordinates before the QWP, after the QWP, and after the HWP, respectively. After demodulation, the reconstructed quantities are denoted by $I_{\textrm{obs}}$ , $Q_{\textrm{obs}}$ , and $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ .

The reconstructed circular polarization signal, $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ , includes the input circular polarization attenuated by the efficiency, together with leakage due to imperfections of the telescope system. We write the relevant response as

$$ V_{\textrm{obs}}=M_{VV}\,V_{\textrm{in}}+M_{IV}\,I_{\textrm{in}}+M_{UV}\,U_{\textrm{in}}+M_{QV}\,Q_{\textrm{in}}, $$

where $M_{VV}$ represents the circular polarization efficiency and the other three coefficients characterize leakage into $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ . Similarly, we define $M_{II}$ and $M_{QQ}$ as the responses from $I_{\textrm{in}}$ to $I_{\textrm{obs}}$ and from $Q_{\textrm{in}}$ to $Q_{\textrm{obs}}$ , respectively. We then define the corresponding leakage coefficients used in the analysis as55 5 The different normalizations are intentional and follow those used in the analysis: the I-to-V leakage is characterized relative to the intensity response, whereas the U-to-V and Q-to-V leakages are characterized relative to the circular-polarization response.

$$ \epsilon_{IV}\equiv\frac{M_{IV}}{M_{II}}\>,\qquad\epsilon_{UV}\equiv\frac{M_{UV}}{M_{VV}}\>,\qquad\epsilon_{QV}\equiv\frac{M_{QV}}{M_{VV}}\>. $$

The circular polarization efficiency $M_{VV}$ can be related to the linear polarization efficiency, $M_{QQ}$ , which is particularly useful because a celestial calibrator with strong, well-known circular polarization is not available. Here, we assume that the efficiencies for Stokes $Q$ and $V$ differ only by the QWP response. For the telescope optics, the cross-polarization is sufficiently small, and thus the telescope response can be approximated as a common efficiency factor for all the Stokes parameters. For the receiver, the cryostat optics are approximately rotationally symmetric and the detector polarization-angle distribution has no strong directional bias. Thus, after averaging over detectors, the polarization efficiency can be approximated as being the same for Stokes $Q$ and $U$ . Denoting the polarization efficiency independent of the QWP by $\eta_{P}$ , the efficiencies for $V$ and $Q$ can then be written as

$$ \displaystyle M_{VV}\equiv\eta_{V} \displaystyle=\eta_{VU}\,\eta_{P}\>, \displaystyle M_{QQ}\equiv\eta_{Q} \displaystyle=\eta_{QQ}\,\eta_{P}\>, $$

where $\eta_{ij}$ is the efficiency with which Stokes $i$ is converted into Stokes $j$ by the QWP. In terms of the QWP Mueller-matrix elements defined in eq. (3), $\eta_{QQ}=T$ and $\eta_{VU}=\eta$ . Thus, $M_{VV}$ can be determined by combining the on-sky calibration of $M_{QQ}$ with the laboratory measurement of the QWP response:

$$ M_{VV}=M_{QQ}\,\frac{\eta_{VU}}{\eta_{QQ}}=M_{QQ}\,\frac{\eta}{T}\>. $$

The U-to-V response, $M_{UV}$ , is characterized on sky using Tau A. The non-ideal QWP response is expected to dominate this term. Neglecting other contributions, it can be written as

$$ M_{UV}\equiv\eta_{U}=\eta_{UU}\,\eta_{P}, $$

where $\eta_{UU}=\epsilon$ in eq. (3). The corresponding U-to-V leakage is therefore

$$ \epsilon_{UV}=\frac{M_{UV}}{M_{VV}}=\frac{\eta_{UU}}{\eta_{VU}}=\frac{\epsilon}{\eta}\>. $$

This relation allows the laboratory QWP measurement to provide an estimate of the U-to-V leakage for comparison with the on-sky characterization.

The I-to-V response, $M_{IV}$ , is not present in the QWP Mueller matrix of eq. (3), but can result from other instrumental effects, including detector non-linearity. This term is corrected on an observation-by-observation basis, and its main impact on the final measurement is the uncertainty associated with the correction (sections 4.1 and 5.1). Similarly, the QWP Mueller matrix does not contain a Q-to-V term. Given the small telescope cross-polarization, the relevant $M_{QV}$ contribution is dominated by polarization-angle miscalibration in the receiver. This effect is subdominant compared to the other systematics (section 5.2.2).

With the $M_{IV}$ term corrected on an observation-by-observation basis and the subdominant $M_{QV}$ term neglected, the observed signal $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ can be related to the sky signal as

$$ V_{\textrm{obs}}=\eta_{V}\,V_{\textrm{sky}}+\epsilon_{UV}\,\eta_{V}\,P_{\textrm{sky}}\,\sin(2\alpha), $$

where $P_{\textrm{sky}}\equiv\sqrt{Q_{\textrm{sky}}^{2}+U_{\textrm{sky}}^{2}}$ is the linear polarization in sky coordinates and $\alpha=\gamma-\alpha_{\rm obs}+\pi/2$ is the angle of the source linear polarization in telescope coordinates. Here, $\gamma$ and $\alpha_{\rm obs}$ are the source polarization angle and the observation’s parallactic angle, respectively. The U-to-V leakage contribution depends on the source parallactic angle, while a sky $V$ signal is constant with parallactic angle. This dependence allows us to characterize the leakage (section 5.2.2) as well as to mitigate the leakage through scan strategy (Paper II).

For the remainder of this paper, we adopt the overall response normalization such that the Stokes $I$ efficiency of the system excluding the QWP is unity. With this convention, $M_{II}=\eta_{II}=T$ . This choice does not affect the quantities considered in this analysis or those reported in Paper II, since they are constructed from ratios of Stokes signals or response coefficients, such as polarization fractions and leakage coefficients, for which a common overall normalization cancels. Accordingly, $\eta_{P}$ represents the polarization efficiency of the system excluding the QWP relative to its Stokes $I$ efficiency. The source circular-polarization fraction reported in this paper and Paper II is expressed in terms of the equivalent sky signal; after accounting for the leakage terms in the measured ratio $V_{\textrm{obs}}/I_{\textrm{obs}}$ , the resulting ratio is divided by the relative response $M_{VV}/M_{II}=\eta\,\eta_{P}/T$ .

## 3 Dataset

We installed the QWP in December 2023, and PB-2b observations were conducted from December 2023 to September 2024. Tau A and Jupiter were observed for calibration during this period. Because the observed circular polarization can be written as the sum of the source circular polarization and leakages (equation (10)), observations with multiple parallactic angles allow us to calibrate the U-to-V leakage and polarization efficiency.

Observation conditions are similar to PB-2a scans. First, we apply the Sun and Moon avoidance. We observed point sources when their positions were more than 15 degrees from the Sun and Moon to avoid contamination through the sidelobe. Then, we operate the telescope at an elevation between 30 and 60 degrees. It is high enough not to pick up signals from the ground and not too high compared to the elevation during tuning, which is approximately 40 degrees.

Some of the radio point sources are observed both when they are rising and setting, which means we observe them with multiple parallactic angles. One observation is about 1 to 1.5 hours long. The scan pattern is called a raster scan. It scans in azimuth back and forth while tracking in elevation. One azimuth sweep is referred to as a subscan. The duration of one subscan is about 15 seconds. The scan speed is $0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{d}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{g}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{c}$ on the sky.

A total of 114 Tau A observations were conducted. From that data, we cut observations with known instrumental issues, bad precipitable water vapor (PWV) conditions, or the number of detectors $<20$ after data selection (see section 4). The final number of observations is 19, which is about 17% of the total observations. Jupiter was continuously observed for commissioning purposes since first light. The number of Jupiter observations with the QWP installed is 48. Applying the same observation selection criteria as Tau A, we use 10 observations (21%) for this analysis.

In addition to Tau A and Jupiter, we observe seven radio point sources, which are RCW 38, IRAS 16183-4958, IRAS 19078+0901, RCW 122, Cen A, 3C 279, and 3C 273. These results are presented in Paper II.

## 4 Analysis

Tau A and Jupiter datasets are analyzed to validate the overall pipeline and evaluate systematic effects. Since we have the HWP rotating at $2\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ , the raw time-ordered data (TOD) is modulated at $8\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ , four times the HWP rotation frequency. We reconstruct the intensity and polarization by demodulation. After calibrating the TOD, we make flat sky maps to estimate the circular polarization fraction. We calculate the fraction of the observed Stokes $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ to the intensity $I_{\textrm{obs}}$ of the sources. The overall pipeline is similar to those used for linear polarization analysis, PB-2a Tau A analysis, for example Adkins et al. (2026).

### 4.1 Data processing

The rotating HWP modulates polarization signals in the detector TOD. The measured modulated signal of a single detector is written as

$$ d_{m}=I_{\textrm{conv}}+\eta_{P}\textrm{Re}[{(Q_{\textrm{conv}}+iU_{\textrm{conv}})m(\chi)e^{i2\theta_{\textrm{det}}}}]+A(\chi)+N_{w}, $$

where $I_{\textrm{conv}}$ , $Q_{\textrm{conv}}$ , and $U_{\textrm{conv}}$ are the incoming Stokes parameters to the HWP Kusaka and others (2014); Takakura et al. (2017). As shown in figure 7, they correspond to the Stokes parameters after conversion by the QWP. Here, $\chi$ is the HWP angle, $\eta_{P}$ is the linear polarization efficiency of the entire system excluding that of the QWP (section 2.4.2), $m(\chi)=\exp(-i4\chi)$ is the modulation function, and $\theta_{\textrm{det}}$ is the detector angle in telescope coordinates. $A(\chi)$ is the spurious modulation signal that correlates with the HWP angle, which is referred to as the HWP synchronous signals (HWPSSs). $N_{w}$ is the detector white noise Kusaka and others (2014). The HWPSS is removed from the TOD as a contaminant, while its phase is also used to calibrate the detector orientation relative to the QWP (section 4.3).

The HWPSS can be expressed by two components, one of which is independent of the sky intensity and the other which is proportional to it, as

$$ A(\chi)=A_{0}(\chi)+\lambda(\chi)\,{I_{\textrm{obs}}}. $$

Each component is decomposed as

$$ \displaystyle A_{0}(\chi) \displaystyle=\sum_{n}(A_{n}^{\prime}\cos(n\chi)+B_{n}^{\prime}\sin(n\chi)) \displaystyle\lambda(\chi) \displaystyle=\sum_{n}(\lambda_{n}^{r}\cos(n\chi)+\lambda_{n}^{i}\sin(n\chi)), $$

where subscript $n$ denotes the $n$ th harmonic and $\chi$ again is the HWP rotation angle. The optical elements of the sky side of the HWP generate the HWPSS Takakura et al. (2017); Kusaka and others (2014). Since we have off-axis mirrors and the birefringent QWP, the fourth harmonic of HWPSS ( $4f$ HWPSS), which is aligned to the QWP and mirror directions, is dominant. We subtract the HWPSS in TOD by calculating the HWPSS amplitude vs. the HWP angle. First, we make an HWPSS model from TOD in each detector. Then, we reconstruct the time vs. HWPSS model using the HWP encoder angle. Finally, we subtract the HWPSS model from the timestreams. This HWPSS is calculated in each subscan considering the HWP fluctuation. The typical HWPSS temperature is found to be about $2\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ . The TOD scanning over the source region is masked when making the HWPSS model, with a circular mask of diameter 0.5 deg around the source.

We demodulate the modulated signal, $d_{m}$ , to reconstruct the incoming signals to the HWP. The intensity is reconstructed by applying lowpass filtering. We apply the filter at $3.8\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ to avoid picking up a significant $4f$ HWPSS described later in this section. To obtain the polarization signals, we apply a bandpass filter around the modulation frequency of $8\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ and then demodulate the TOD by multiplying the complex conjugate of the modulation function $m(\chi)$ . We then apply a lowpass filter to the demodulated TOD. The real and imaginary parts of the lowpass-filtered TOD correspond to the incoming Stokes $Q$ and $U$ parameters, $Q_{\rm conv}$ and $U_{\rm conv}$ , respectively. The reconstructed polarization signals, $Q_{\textrm{obs}}$ and $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ , can be written in terms of $Q_{\textrm{in}}$ , $U_{\textrm{in}}$ , and $V_{\textrm{in}}$ as described in section 2.4.2:

$$ \displaystyle Q_{\textrm{obs}} \displaystyle\simeq\eta_{Q}\,Q_{\textrm{in}} \displaystyle V_{\textrm{obs}} \displaystyle\simeq\eta_{V}\,V_{\textrm{in}}+\eta_{U}\,U_{\textrm{in}}. $$

The leakage in the demodulated signal proportional to the unpolarized intensity is so-called intensity-to-polarization (I-to-P) leakage. There are two kinds of leakage relevant to this analysis, “I-to-Q leakage” and “I-to-V leakage.” The I-to-Q leakage is the leakage to the $Q$ signal in the telescope frame. It is caused by imperfections of optical elements like the QWP and non-linearity of the detectors Takakura et al. (2017). On the other hand, the I-to-V leakage can arise from the non-linearity of the time constant of detectors. The time constant has temporal variations during the observation. The variations proportional to the incoming signal fluctuations generate an imaginary component in the demodulated signals Takakura et al. (2017). The QWP itself does not make the I-to-V leakage (section 2.3). We subtract the leakage in timestreams. We follow the PB-2a Tau A analysis method Adkins et al. (2026), which uses low-frequency atmospheric fluctuations to estimate the leakage coefficients Takakura et al. (2017); Johnson et al. (2007). We calculate the I-to-Q and I-to-V leakage coefficients, $\lambda_{4}^{r}$ and $\lambda_{4}^{i}$ , respectively, from the correlation between the low-frequency fluctuations in the intensity and polarization timestreams Takakura et al. (2017). Here, $\lambda_{4}^{i}$ corresponds to the I-to-V leakage coefficient $\epsilon_{IV}$ defined in section 2.4.2. The coefficients are calculated in the time domain after lowpass filtering at $0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ per subscan. Further discussion of systematic uncertainties due to this leakage is in section 5.1.

We apply polynomial filters to the demodulated TOD, to remove the long-timescale fluctuations of the atmosphere and instruments. We apply a third-order polynomial filter to both intensity and polarization in each subscan, with the source masked out using the same 0.5-degree-diameter circular mask Collaboration (2020b); Collaboration (2014).

### 4.2 Data selection

We apply two types of data selections, “observation selection” and “detector selection.” Regarding observation selections, we choose the observations based on the specific observation conditions. The criteria are similar to those of PB-1 Tau A and PB-2a Tau A analysis Collaboration (2024); Adkins et al. (2026). After excluding observations with known instrumental problems, we select observations with favorable weather conditions. The criteria are that the average PWV $<4$ mm and (Max PWV - Min PWV) $<$ $1\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ over the course of the observation. The PWV data comes from the Atacama Pathfinder EXperiment (APEX) radiometer Güsten et al. (2006). It is located about $5\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{m}$ southeast of the SA telescopes. Additionally, we select observations that have more than 20 detectors after the detector selections described below. The final number of Tau A observations that meet these selection criteria is 19.

The detector selection is divided into two parts. The first part is the selection common to observations. Of all PB-2b’s detectors, we select those that are sensitive to $90\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ and have pointing offset information Russell et al. (2024). The number of these detectors is 1018.

The second part is performed observation by observation. This is run during the data processing, which means that we apply the data selection for each TOD. It is divided into four steps. The first is the tuning status. We selected the successfully tuned bolometers for each observation. Next, we verify whether the selected detectors can detect optical signals. We utilize the HWPSS for this selection. To characterize the HWPSS (Equation (12)), we fit the HWPSS angle vs. amplitude in TOD as

$$ A_{0}=\sum_{n=1}^{6}A^{\prime}_{n}\sin(n\chi)+B^{\prime}_{n}\cos(n\chi), $$

where the amplitude of the $n$ -th harmonic is $A_{n}=\sqrt{A_{n}^{\prime 2}+B_{n}^{\prime 2}}$ . The data selection is conducted with the fourth harmonic amplitude. We normalize the $A_{4}$ by the RMS of fit residuals. We select detectors that have $>10$ HWPSS SNR.

Then, we select the bolometers based on a spectrogram. A baseline drift occurs randomly due to issues such as detector non-linearity, so we check for no drift around the target source. We calculate the mean power lower than $3.8\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ in the Fourier domain. Figure 8 shows an example of the spectrogram analysis. The power is calculated in every subscan, and we define the outlier point as

$$ P_{i}-\textrm{median}(P_{i})>10\times\textrm{median}(|P_{i}-\textrm{median}(P_{i})|), $$

where $P_{i}$ is the $i$ -th subscan mean power lower than $3.8\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ . The TOD is masked while scanning the source region. We select detectors that show no outliers when the source is hitting. This criterion requires the absence of outliers in the subscan containing the source and in the surrounding $\pm 5$ subscans.

Finally, we cut detectors based on I-to-P leakage coefficients. The coefficient of I-to-P leakage is calculated as a median of each subscan coefficient. However, some of the coefficients in a single observation exhibit significant variations. To select detectors with stable leakage coefficients, we set the criteria as

$$ \frac{Q3-Q1}{2}<0.03. $$

Here, $Q1$ ( $Q3$ ) represents the first (third) quartile of the leakage coefficients of each detector during an observation, where the leakage is calculated in each subscan. While this leakage cut is the largest hit to the data selection, it is necessary to limit the uncertainty introduced by the I-to-V leakage correction. This correction is the largest source of systematic uncertainty in the final circular polarization measurement (section 5.2.2; see also Paper II), and the cut is needed to maintain a balance between systematic and statistical uncertainties. In particular, this selection limits fluctuations in the leakage correction by requiring the leakage coefficient to be stable within each observation, rather than selecting on the measured source polarization.

### 4.3 Calibration

There are four types of detectors, each group sensitive to microwaves with different polarization directions, in each wafer on the focal plane. After demodulation, we rotate the detector angle to reconstruct polarizations and obtain $Q_{\textrm{obs}}$ and $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ maps on the telescope coordinates. We find that the HWPSS is significant compared to the sky signal, about $2\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , after installing the QWP, and we utilize it for calibration. The HWPSS is aligned to the QWP vertical axis, which is the same as the mirror polarization direction.66 6 We confirm it by comparing angles between observations with and without the QWP. We also check angles using Tau A to confirm no obvious angle miscalibration. The angle of the detectors is calculated using the phase of the fourth harmonic of the HWPSS, which reflects the QWP’s physical orientation. It is calculated in each observation considering the time constant variation. Note that this analysis does not need the absolute detector polarization angle.

The detector pointing offsets are calculated from planet scans Russell et al. (2024). We use this array pointing for all observations to make source-centered maps.

Gain is the detector’s responsivity to the input signals. Since we report the circular polarization ratio to intensity, we only calibrate the gain between detectors, which is called relative gain. We use the fourth-harmonic amplitude of the HWPSS, assuming that detectors see the same HWPSS.

One of the biggest systematics of this analysis is the leakage. We developed the leakage subtraction and uncertainty estimation method from Tau A and Jupiter observations. Details are discussed in section 5.

### 4.4 Map making and noise characterization

From the demodulated TOD, we create maps of intensity and polarizations. The mapmaking pipeline is similar to PB-2a analysis Adkins et al. (2026). Our map is a source-centered map using the detector pointing offset in telescope coordinates. The map is pixelized to $0.02\text{\,}\mathrm{d}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{g}\,$ $\times$ $0.02\text{\,}\mathrm{d}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{g}\,$ per pixel. The reconstructed $I_{\textrm{obs}}$ and $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ signals are projected onto maps and coadded with inverse-noise weights. We denote the resulting coadded intensity and circular-polarization maps by $I_{\textrm{coadd}}$ and $V_{\textrm{coadd}}$ , respectively.

The measured circular-polarization fraction is calculated from these coadded maps by integrating pixels within a 0.1-degree radius as

$$ V_{\textrm{frac}}=\frac{\Sigma_{p}^{r<0.1}V_{\textrm{coadd},p}}{\Sigma_{p}^{r<0.1}I_{\textrm{coadd},p}}, $$

where $I_{\textrm{coadd},p}$ and $V_{\textrm{coadd},p}$ are the $p$ th $I_{\textrm{coadd}}$ and $V_{\textrm{coadd}}$ map pixels in the coadded map. Thus, $V_{\textrm{frac}}$ is the map-domain counterpart of $V_{\textrm{obs}}/I_{\textrm{obs}}$ , obtained after reconstructing $V_{\textrm{obs}}$ and $I_{\textrm{obs}}$ into maps and integrating over the source region.

The statistical uncertainty is estimated from the map. Figure 9 (left) shows the regions from an example noise map used for noise estimation. Noise estimate regions are defined as having a 0.1-degree radius with the centers of ( $\pm 0.25,0$ ), ( $0,\pm 0.25$ ), and ( $\pm 0.25,\pm 0.25$ ) degree. We perform two methods for noise calculation and compare the results.
