- • Method A: RMS of eight regions This method calculates the mean of each circle of the map first (figure 9) and then calculates the root mean square (RMS) of eight values. It is described as

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\times\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{8}\left(\frac{\sum_{i\in C_{j}}v_{i}}{N_{C_{j}}}\right)^{2}}, $$

(20) where $v_{i}$ is the value of pixel $i$ , $C_{j}$ is the circle $j$ ( $j=1,2,...,8$ ), and $N_{C_{j}}$ is the number of pixels in $C_{j}$ . This method directly accounts for the correlations among map pixels, but its statistical uncertainty is large because only eight regions are available.

- • Method B: RMS of all pixels in eight regions This method calculates the RMS of all pixels in noise regions. It is described as

$$ \mathcal{N}_{B}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{C_{s}}}}\times\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i\in C}v_{i}^{2}}{N_{C}}}, $$

(21) where $v_{i}$ again is the value of pixel $i$ , $N_{C}$ is the number of pixels of all noise calculated regions, and $N_{C_{s}}$ is the number of pixels in the signal calculated region. This method has a significantly smaller statistical error than method A, thanks to the approximately 700 pixels. However, the noise level of method B is underestimated due to pixel correlation in the azimuth direction, which is the telescope’s scan direction. This can be seen in figure 9. Both blue and red pixels appear to be horizontally connected by about three pixels along the $x$ axis, whereas the $y$ axis is not, indicating a correlation in the azimuth direction.

As our final noise estimate, we calculate the ratio between the two methods for all detectors across all observations. We then take the median of them and multiply it by $\mathcal{N}_{B}$ as

$$ \mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}_{B}\times\mathrm{median}(\mathcal{N}_{A}/\mathcal{N}_{B}). $$

Figure 9 (right) shows the histogram of the ratio of two methods of Tau A observations. The median value is about 1.8 for Tau A, which is consistent with Jupiter and other sources reported in Paper II. The value is reasonable considering the number of correlated pixels in figure 9. Here, $\mathcal{N}$ represents the statistical uncertainty in the mean $V_{\textrm{coadd}}$ signal within the source region. The statistical uncertainty in $V_{\textrm{frac}}$ can then be expressed as

$$ \sigma_{\textrm{stat}}=\frac{\mathcal{N}}{I_{\textrm{source}}}\>, $$

where the mean observed source intensity is defined as $I_{\textrm{source}}=\sum_{p}^{r<0.1}I_{\textrm{coadd},p}/N_{C_{s}}$ .

## 5 Results

The goal of this analysis is to determine calibration parameters and characterize the uncertainties relevant to circular polarization measurements. As demonstrated in figure 7, our telescope optics with the addition of the QWP allow us to obtain data for intensity, for one linear polarization (Stokes $Q$ ) and for circular polarization (Stokes $V$ ). We utilize both polarizations for validating our telescope and conducting systematics studies of astronomical sources. Jupiter observations are used for I-to-V leakage validation, and Tau A observations are used for linear polarization efficiency and U-to-V leakage estimations. I-to-V leakage uncertainty estimated from Jupiter observations is also validated with the Tau A observations. Note that Q-to-V leakage is negligibly small in this analysis, as described in section 5.2.2.

### 5.1 Jupiter observations

We use Jupiter observations to verify our overall pipeline and estimate the systematic uncertainty associated with the I-to-V leakage correction. It is a bright, compact point source widely used for telescope calibration, and its linear polarization is negligible for this work. Figure 10 shows the maps of one Jupiter observation with and without I-to-P leakage subtractions. We find that the leakage is successfully removed in the maps as a result of the data processing described in section 4.1. The typical value of the I-to-Q (I-to-V) leakage is about 6% (1%). These values are larger than those for the PB-1 or PB-2a telescopes due to the QWP, but are reasonable considering that the QWP has about $2\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ HWPSS Takakura et al. (2017).

*Figure 10: Jupiter maps with and without I-to-P leakage subtraction. Maps are coadded over the detectors of one observation. From left to right, observed intensity, linear polarization, and circular polarization are shown. The top row shows the map without the leakage subtraction, and the bottom row shows the map after subtraction. The color scale is normalized by Jupiter intensity. The comparison demonstrates that the leakage subtraction removes the dominant I-to-P leakage structure.*

The relevant systematic associated with the I-to-V leakage is not the leakage itself, which is corrected observation by observation, but the uncertainty in that correction. Since the source intensity is much brighter than the typical circular polarization level, even a small misestimation of the leakage coefficient can produce a significant uncertainty in the final circular polarization measurement. The uncertainty in the I-to-V leakage correction has a statistical nature, showing detector-to-detector and observation-to-observation variation rather than behaving as a fixed bias. This is consistent with its origin in detector non-linearity (section 4.1). We therefore establish a model to estimate this uncertainty, assuming that Jupiter’s circular polarization remains constant during our observation period. The same model is applied to Tau A and other point sources, and its validity is supported by the Tau A analysis presented below and by the null test results in Paper II.

We model the uncertainty associated with the I-to-V leakage correction empirically using the Jupiter observations. As defined in section 4.4, $V_{\textrm{frac}}$ is the map-domain counterpart of $V_{\textrm{obs}}/I_{\textrm{obs}}$ , and its statistical uncertainty $\sigma_{\textrm{stat}}$ is given by eq. (23). Since the low-frequency atmospheric intensity fluctuations used for the leakage estimate are approximately independent of the observed source, we assume that the uncertainty in the I-to-V leakage coefficient scales with $\mathcal{N}\,(=\sigma_{\textrm{stat}}\,I_{\textrm{source}})$ , the statistical uncertainty in the source $V$ measurement. Thus, we model the I-to-V leakage-correction uncertainty in $V_{\textrm{frac}}$ as

$$ \sigma_{\textrm{ItoV}}=B\,\frac{I_{\textrm{source}}}{I_{\textrm{Jupiter}}}\,\sigma_{\textrm{stat}}\>, $$

where $B$ is a source-independent proportionality factor and $I_{\textrm{Jupiter}}$ is the mean observed Jupiter intensity defined in the same manner as $I_{\textrm{source}}$ . We also note that the I-to-V leakage-correction uncertainty is directly related to the uncertainty in the leakage coefficient as $\sigma_{\textrm{ItoV}}=\sigma(\epsilon_{IV})$ , since an error $\delta\epsilon_{IV}$ in the leakage coefficient produces a residual $\delta V_{\textrm{obs}}=\delta\epsilon_{IV}\,I_{\textrm{obs}}$ , and hence $\delta(V_{\textrm{obs}}/I_{\textrm{obs}})=\delta\epsilon_{IV}$ .

The factor $B$ is determined using Jupiter observations by comparing two observation-level estimates of the I-to-V leakage coefficient Collaboration (2024). The first estimate is based on low-frequency fluctuations of the TOD and is used in the nominal data processing for the TOD-level leakage correction (section 4.1); it is an estimate of the per-detector, per-observation leakage coefficient $\lambda_{4}^{i}$ in eq. (14). For the comparison here, we calculate, for each observation $o$ , the weighted mean of the estimated $\lambda_{4}^{i}$ over detectors and denote the resulting detector-averaged coefficient as $\bar{\lambda}_{4,o}^{i}$ . The second estimate is used only for Jupiter and serves here to characterize the uncertainty in the first estimate. It uses the Jupiter intensity and circular polarization maps. For each observation, we calculate the leakage coefficient from the detector-coadded Jupiter map by integrating the map within a 0.1-degree radius, and denote it as $\bar{\lambda}_{4_{\textrm{Jupiter}},o}^{i}$ .77 7 We use the bar to distinguish the detector-averaged quantities for each observation, $\bar{\lambda}_{4_{\textrm{Jupiter}},o}^{i}$ and $\bar{\lambda}_{4,o}^{i}$ , from the per-detector, per-observation leakage coefficient, $\lambda_{4}^{i}$ , for which the detector and observation indices are omitted. The left panel of figure 11 shows an example of the comparison for one observation, demonstrating good agreement between the two estimates.

At the individual-observation level, the uncertainty represented by $\sigma(\epsilon_{IV})$ corresponds to the uncertainty in $\bar{\lambda}_{4,o}^{i}$ . Thus, applying $B=\sigma(\epsilon_{IV})/\sigma_{\textrm{stat}}$ to each observation, we estimate the factor $B$ as

$$ B=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{o}\left(\frac{\bar{\lambda}_{4,o}^{i}-\bar{\lambda}_{4_{\textrm{Jupiter}},o}^{i}}{\sigma_{\textrm{stat},o}}\right)^{2}}\>, $$

where $\sigma_{\textrm{stat},o}$ is the statistical uncertainty in $V_{\textrm{frac}}$ defined in eq. (23) for Jupiter observation $o$ , and $N$ is the number of Jupiter observations. The right panel of figure 11 shows the distribution of the normalized differences entering this calculation, which yields $B=18.8$ . The resulting uncertainty model in eq. (24) is then applied to each source using its measured intensity relative to Jupiter. For Tau A, the measured intensity ratio gives $B\,(I_{\textrm{obs,TauA}}/I_{\textrm{obs,Jupiter}})=2.8$ .

Several factors contribute to the inefficiency of the linear polarization measurement. One contribution comes from optics, including the HWP and QWP. From the Mueller matrix calculation based on lab measurements, the efficiency of the HWP with AR coatings is $>99$ %. The QWP does not reduce the linear-polarization efficiency relative to its intensity transmission (eq. (3)). Thus, this combination suggests the efficiency $>99$ %. Another instrument factor is the detector. Our receiver has lenslet-coupled sinuous antenna transition edge sensor bolometer arrays. The polarization efficiency of detectors is suggested to be about 95% Westbrook et al. (2018). Additionally, the detector time constant reduces the response. The efficiency is about 80%88 8 While we do not explicitly deconvolve the detector time constant in the TOD analysis, its dominant effects are effectively accounted for through calibration. The attenuation of the modulated signal amplitude is absorbed into the overall polarization efficiency calibration using Tau A. The associated phase shift, which appears as an effective detector polarization angle rotation and could otherwise lead to leakage or calibration bias if it varies between observations, is mitigated through the observation-by-observation detector angle calibration using the HWPSS (section 4.3)., assuming the time constant $\tau$ of $15\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ Takakura et al. (2017). PB-2b time constant without the QWP is reported to be around $12\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ Farias et al. (2025). Inefficiency can also be introduced during offline analysis, especially by TOD filtering. We apply filters in the reconstruction of intensity and polarization maps. To estimate this effect, we simulate an ideal noise-free Tau A signal using the actual Tau A scan information. The same TOD filters and mapmaking procedure are then applied as in the real data analysis. The resulting polarization efficiency of the TOD filtering and mapmaking process is about 97%. Despite considering all the possible contributions discussed above, the observed inefficiency cannot be fully explained. As an additional check, we compared the detector physical angles with and without the QWP and obtained consistent results. A separate Tau A observation without the QWP yielded an efficiency of about 50%. These checks further support the treatment in eq. (7), in which the measured Stokes- $Q$ efficiency is related to the Stokes- $V$ efficiency through the QWP conversion factor. A complete accounting of the observed inefficiency is left for future work.

The measured linear polarization efficiency can be related to that of circular polarization via $\eta_{V}=\eta_{Q}\,(\eta_{VU}/\eta_{QQ})$ according to the polarization optics model described in section 2.4.2. As illustrated schematically in figure 7, $\eta_{QQ}$ and $\eta_{VU}$ are determined by the QWP properties and correspond to $T$ and $\eta$ in eq. (3), respectively. Their ratio, $\eta_{VU}/\eta_{QQ}=\eta/T$ , was measured to be 99.0% from the laboratory characterization of the QWP (section 2.3.2). At the current level of precision, this correction is negligible. We therefore adopt the measured efficiency of $46\pm 2$ % as the circular polarization efficiency.

#### 5.2.2 Leakage calibration

Tau A circular polarization measurement is utilized to characterize U-to-V leakages and to validate the uncertainty associated with the I-to-V leakage correction estimated from Jupiter observations. Tau A circular polarization at $90\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ is reported to be $<0.2$ % Wiesemeyer et al. (2011). The uncertainty induced by the I-to-V leakage correction is further supported by the null test results for the other sources presented in Paper II.

Figure 13 (right) shows the measured circular polarization fraction, $V_{\textrm{frac}}$ , of the Tau A observations as a function of parallactic angle, together with the fit. Dividing eq. (10) by $I_{\textrm{obs}}=M_{II}I_{\textrm{sky}}$ gives

$$ \frac{V_{\textrm{obs}}}{I_{\textrm{obs}}}=\frac{M_{VV}}{M_{II}}\left[\frac{V_{\textrm{sky}}}{I_{\textrm{sky}}}+\epsilon_{UV}\frac{P_{\textrm{sky}}}{I_{\textrm{sky}}}\sin(2\alpha)\right], $$

where $M_{VV}/M_{II}=\eta\,\eta_{P}/T$ as described in section 2.4.2. We fit the data with two free parameters: a constant offset and the amplitude of the sinusoidal component. The constant offset is converted to the Tau A circular polarization fraction using the calibrated relative response $M_{VV}/M_{II}$ . The sinusoidal amplitude is converted to the U-to-V leakage coefficient using the same relative response together with the known Tau A linear polarization fraction. The fit yields a circular polarization fraction consistent with zero and a nonzero best-fit U-to-V leakage, as discussed below.

We apply the I-to-V leakage-correction uncertainty model derived from Jupiter observations to the Tau A fit. The uncertainty used in the fit after including the I-to-V leakage-correction uncertainty, denoted by $\sigma^{\prime}$ , is given by

$$ \sigma^{\prime}=\sqrt{\sigma_{\textrm{stat}}^{2}+\sigma_{\textrm{ItoV}}^{2}}=\sigma_{\textrm{stat}}\sqrt{1+B^{2}\left(\frac{I_{\textrm{source}}}{I_{\textrm{Jupiter}}}\right)^{2}}\>. $$

The resulting fit has a reduced chi-squared of 0.85, indicating that the assigned uncertainty is consistent with the observed scatter. For comparison, the fit to the data without I-to-V leakage subtraction has a reduced chi-squared of 3.96. This comparison supports both the I-to-V leakage correction and the associated uncertainty model derived from Jupiter observations. We use this uncertainty model in the other point-source analyses as well (Paper II).

The fitted U-to-V leakage is $\epsilon_{UV}=-11.7\pm 5.1$ %. The value is consistent with that from the QWP lab measurement, which is $-7.2\%$ (see section 2.3.2). Although the measured leakage is at the approximately 10% level, its impact is reduced for sources with small linear polarization. The effect of U-to-V leakage can also be mitigated by the scan strategy (see Paper II). The measured circular polarization fraction of Tau A is $0.78\pm 0.42$ %. This value does not indicate a significant detection of circular polarization in Tau A, which is consistent with the previous publication Wiesemeyer et al. (2011).

The Q-to-V leakage is expected to be much smaller than the U-to-V leakage. A detector angle miscalibration can rotate Stokes $Q$ into the detector-frame $U$ component. In the absence of such miscalibration, Stokes $V$ is converted by the QWP into the detector-frame $U$ component. Thus, the angle miscalibration appears as an effective Q-to-V leakage. The Stokes $Q$ and $U$ in this context are defined in the coordinate system of the QWP birefringence axis. Since our detector polarization angle calibration uses the HWPSS, which primarily arises from the QWP differential emissivity aligned with this axis, this type of angle miscalibration is intrinsically suppressed. A small residual miscalibration can arise from the secondary HWPSS contribution due to polarization generated by the off-axis reflector telescope optics, but only when the telescope optical axis is misaligned with respect to the QWP birefringence axis. The measured residual QWP misalignment at the site is $<0.3^{\circ}$ (section 2.4.1), corresponding to an effective Q-to-V leakage of less than 1.1%, an order of magnitude smaller than the measured U-to-V leakage. We therefore neglect this effect in the analysis.

## 6 Conclusion

We have developed and characterized a method to search for circular polarization at millimeter wavelengths by incorporating a QWP into the SA PB-2b optical system. The QWP converts incident circular polarization into linear polarization before HWP modulation. This allows Stokes $V$ to be measured with the PB-2b’s TES-bolometer-equipped receiver and its associated analysis pipeline, requiring only minor modifications to the existing infrastructure. Laboratory measurements give a QWP conversion efficiency, $\eta/T$ , of 99.0% in the $90\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ band.

Using Jupiter and Tau A observations, we have established a calibration scheme and quantified the systematic uncertainties, including those associated with I-to-V and U-to-V leakage. Jupiter observations are used to establish the I-to-V leakage-correction uncertainty model, including its scaling with source intensity relative to Jupiter. The assigned uncertainty is supported by the Tau A circular-polarization fit. The linear polarization measurements of Tau A confirm the overall consistency of our pipeline and provide an estimate of the effective polarization efficiency. The estimated polarization efficiency adopted for Stokes $V$ is $46\pm 2$ %, and the measured U-to-V leakage is $\epsilon_{UV}=-11.7\pm 5.1$ %. The Q-to-V leakage is estimated to be less than 1.1% and is neglected in the analysis. The circular polarization results show no significant detection for Tau A, with $V/I=0.78\pm 0.42$ %, which is consistent with the literature Wiesemeyer et al. (2011). The calibration products established in this paper, including the Stokes- $V$ efficiency, I-to-V leakage-correction uncertainty prescription, U-to-V leakage characterization, and Q-to-V treatment, are applied to the circular-polarization search of other astronomical sources presented in Paper II The POLARBEAR Collaboration ().

In addition to the point-source observations, we also obtained CMB observation data with PB-2b for circular-polarization analysis. More broadly, the QWP-based method developed here may be applicable to other CMB polarization experiments, such as the Simons Observatory, that are primarily designed for linear-polarization measurements. The addition of a QWP provides a way to extend such systems to circular-polarization measurements with relatively minor modifications to the existing instrumentation and analysis framework.

## Abstract

We developed a broadband two-layer anti-reflection (AR) coating for use on a sapphire half-wave plate (HWP) and an alumina infrared (IR) filter for the cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarimetry. Measuring the faint CMB B-mode signals requires maximizing the number of photons reaching the detectors and minimizing spurious polarization due to reflection with an off-axis incident angle. Sapphire and alumina have high refractive indices of 3.1 and are highly reflective without an AR coating. This paper presents the design, fabrication, quality control, and measured performance of an AR coating using thermally-sprayed mullite and Duroid 5880LZ. This technology enables large optical elements with diameters of $600\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ . We also present a newly developed thermography-based nondestructive quality control technique, which is key to assuring good adhesion and preventing delamination when thermal cycling. We demonstrate the average reflectance of about 2.6% (0.9%) for two observing bands centered at 90/150 (220/280) GHz. At room temperature, the average transmittance of a $105\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ square test sample at 220/280 GHz is 83%, and it will increase to 90% at $100\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , attributed to reduced absorption losses. Therefore, our developed layering technique has proved effective for 220/280 GHz applications, particularly in addressing dielectric loss concerns. This AR coating technology has been deployed in the cryogenic HWP and IR filters of the Simons Array and the Simons observatory experiments and applies to future experiments such as CMB-S4.

## 1 Introduction

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) provides various information for understanding the early universe, including inflation [1, 2]. In particular, B-mode polarization, the parity-odd polarization anisotropy pattern, is induced by primordial gravitational waves, gravitational lensing, and foregrounds. The existence of primordial gravitational waves is anticipated, but their measurement has not yet been achieved. The measurement of the B-mode polarization signal is challenging because the signal amplitude is expected to be smaller than $10\text{\,}\mathrm{n}$ [3].

Intensity-to-Polarization (I-to-P) leakage is one of the major obstacles to CMB polarization measurements. The magnitude of B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves is considered seven orders of magnitude fainter compared to the unpolarized CMB temperature anisotropy [3, 4, 5]. Minimizing I-to-P leakage caused by the imperfection of the optical elements to a few per mil is crucial. Furthermore, the statistical error has been improved with the growing number of telescope detectors in recent years. Reducing systematic errors to a level lower than the corresponding statistical errors is imperative.

Some of the optical elements, such as a continuously rotating half-wave plate (HWP) and an infrared (IR) filter, have been introduced for high-precision CMB experiments such as the Simons Array (SA) and the Simons Observatory (SO) [6, 7, 8]. An HWP modulates only the polarization signal to mitigate atmospheric 1/f noise and prevents systematics arising from different responses in pairs of polarimeters by rotating continuously [9, 10, 11]. An IR filter blocks infrared radiation that otherwise would heat the cryogenic telescope components. Since IR radiation heats the IR filter, crystalline material, such as alumina, is advantageous for thermal conductivity over a polymer-based filter or a thin membrane. In addition, recent CMB experiments operate at cryogenic temperatures for noise considerations. Implementing these optical elements at cryogenic temperatures is the key to high-precision CMB measurement.

The sapphire and alumina used for HWPs and IR filters have high refractive indices of 3.1 [12, 13], which reflects $\sim 40\%$ of light as they are. Regarding the statistical error, there is a concern about a significant decrease in transmittance because each receiver has multiple optical elements. In addition, high reflectance causes significant I-to-P leakage. The oblique incidence of light into the telescope causes the reflectance to be different for the two orthogonal polarizations, which is a major cause of I-to-P leakage. In particular, polarization from optical elements (e.g., IR filter) on the sky side of the HWP causes a large leakage because the HWP cannot distinguish it from incident polarization. Highly reflective elements increase systematic and statistical uncertainties. Thus, an anti-reflection (AR) coating is critical for these materials.

There are a few challenging aspects of AR coatings for modern CMB instruments. First, applying a coating on 600-mm-diameter alumina surfaces with uniformity of tens of microns is difficult. Second, the SA and SO use dichroic detectors with individual bands with a large, about 30%, fractional bandwidth [14, 15]. Thus, each AR coating must cover over an octave of bandwidth. Finally, the AR-coated optical elements are cooled down to < $80\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ to reduce thermal radiation reaching the cryogenic detectors. It creates challenges associated with differential thermal contraction between coating layers.

Some ways to apply AR coatings, like layering dielectrics or machining sub-wavelength structures, have been reported [16, 17, 18]. Among these methods, we choose layering dielectrics given the difficulty of machining substrates, which are sapphire or alumina, the required machining time for large-diameter substrates, and the difficulty in applying the high-frequency band. We establish the fabrication process of the AR coating by introducing new quality control methods. Our AR coating consists of two dielectric layers. The first layer is thermally sprayed mullite [12], a ceramic material (Tocalo Corporation) [19]. The second layer is Duroid 5880LZ, a composite material (Rogers Corporation) [20], bonded with Epo-Tek 301 [21], a two-component room-temperature curing epoxy. We select these materials for their refractive index and coefficient of thermal expansion. By adjusting the thickness of the coating materials, an AR coating can be optimized for a specific frequency band.

This paper presents the development of broadband multi-layer AR coatings for CMB experiments. Section 2 describes the design. Coating materials are chosen based on the HWP and IR filter requirements. Section 3 presents the materials being fabricated. Section 4 describes the fabrication process and quality control of the coatings, including tests for delamination. Section 5 presents the optical characterization of fabricated coatings. Both reflectance and transmittance measurements are described.

## 2 Design

We decided on a two-layer coating design for a sapphire HWP and an IR filter. Figure 1 shows the schematic of our AR coating. Two layers of mullite and Duroid are coated on alumina surfaces. Details of these materials are written in Section 3. Figure 2 shows the cross-section of a sample taken by X-ray computed tomography (CT). The boundaries of the layers can be seen, and the accuracy of the thickness is $10\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ . Epo-Tek, a glue between mullite and Duroid, is also uniform and has a thickness of about $40\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ .

We primarily discuss the AR coating on alumina since the fabrication process is more robust and mature than the coating on sapphire. As for the sapphire HWP coating, the fabrication process is slightly different. The HWP is made of a stack of three sapphire plates [22]. We first fabricate two one-surface-coated aluminas. We then adhere them to both surfaces of the sapphire stack. All the deployable HWP AR coatings we fabricated to date have been achieved this way. However, as described in Sec. 4.3, applying the AR coating directly on sapphire is also feasible.

### 2.1 HWP and IR filter requirements

We develop the AR coating for ground-based CMB experiments like the SA. The requirements of the HWP and IR filter are described below:

- • The HWP diameter is $500\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ , and the IR filter diameter is about 500 or 600 mm [22, 7]. The AR coating needs to be uniform across this large diameter.

- • The reflectance must be less than a few percent across the detector bands, which typically have $\sim 30$ % fractional bandwidth. In addition, the SA and the SO experiments use dichroic detectors. The AR coating should cover these wide bands. We define two frequency bands, Mid-frequency (MF) and Ultra-high-frequency (UHF), based on the experiment bands [23, 24, 25]. We use 78–106 GHz as MF1, 128–168 GHz as MF2, 195–256 GHz as UHF1, and 257–316 GHz as UHF2 to calculate the average reflectance for each band.

- • Layers of the AR coating must not delaminate when thermally cycled to the cryogenic temperature of 4, 40, or $80\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ [7, 6]. It is thus desirable to have a minimal mismatch of the coefficient of thermal expansion among the AR coating and base materials.

### 2.2 Material choice

While several techniques have been developed and reported in the literature [26, 27, 28], repeatable and scalable production of the large-diameter coating remains challenging. We use a two-layer coating to achieve the required low reflectivity across a broad frequency range.

The coating is optimized by selecting the thicknesses and indices of the two coating layers. As a first-order approximation, the maximum bandwidth of minimal reflection can be achieved when the thickness of each layer is 1/4 wavelength and the indices satisfy:

$$ n_{\rm{s}}=\frac{n_{1}^{2}}{n_{2}^{2}}, $$

where $n_{1}$ , $n_{2}$ , and $n_{s}$ are the indices of the first layer, second layer, and sapphire or alumina, respectively [29]. Considering the index, coefficient of thermal expansion, and compressive modulus, we choose coating materials to meet the above-mentioned requirements.

Figure 1 schematically shows our AR coatings. Mullite ceramic [19] is selected as the first layer, and Duroid 5880LZ [20] filled PTFE composite as the second layer. Mullite had been used as the coating material before [12], but the combination of mullite and Duroid is first used as a coating for an HWP and a filter for the SA and the SO. Details of these materials are mentioned in Section 3.

### 2.3 Parameter optimization

Table 1 shows the design thicknesses of the materials used. The thicknesses are optimized to minimize the average reflectance at normal incidence in each frequency band. Numerical calculations obtain the average reflectance. This prediction is calculated assuming an infinite plane wave incident on a homogeneous dielectric thin layer [30]. The 40 µm-thick layer of Epo-Tek [21] is placed between two coating layers as glue, and its thickness is included in the average reflectance calculation. Epo-Tek does not affect the performance because the index of the Epo-Tek is between that of mullite and Duroid, and the thickness is an order of magnitude smaller than that of coating materials.

We fabricate $$105\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$\times$105\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$$ square samples based on the above calculation. There are differences in coating thickness when we run optical measurements. We hypothesize that the difference between the physical and optical values at the millimeter wave causes the thickness differences. These differences are not a problem in developing an optimal AR coating, as the differences are stable between fabrication runs. The process is repeated by adjusting the thickness of the layers until the optimal coating is obtained.

## 3 Material Summary

### 3.1 Alumina

As a substrate, we use A995LD alumina manufactured by NTK ceratec [32], a low-dielectric-loss type, 99.5% pure alumina with a refractive index of 3.1 at microwave frequencies. It has desirable material properties for an IR filter: low microwave absorption loss, high IR absorption, and high thermal conductivity at cryogenic temperature [33]. It is also used for the AR coating substrate of the sapphire HWP (Fig. 1, right). Since both are crystalline ${\rm Al}_{2}{\rm O}_{3}$ , the indices of sapphire and alumina are well matched as shown in Table 1, and reflectance due to this minor mismatch is negligible. The thickness of alumina is 2–7 mm depending on the application. While thinner alumina is desirable, particularly in the UHF band, for lower absorption and scattering, alumina of $<$3\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$$ thickness with $600\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ diameter does require handling with care.

### 3.2 Sapphire

We use $\alpha$ -cut sapphire plates manufactured at Guizhou Hoatian Optoelectronics Technology (GHTOT) [34] as a cryogenic birefringent substrate for HWPs [6]. We stack three sapphire plates to achieve broadband polarization modulation efficiency [35]. As shown in Table 1, sapphire has a large differential index and small loss tangent [22]. The refractive index of the ordinary (extraordinary) axis is 3.1 (3.4). The MF (UHF) HWP consists of three 3.75-mm-thick (1.6-mm-thick) sapphire plates for optimum modulation efficiency across the frequency band and practicality [22, 35].

### 3.3 Mullite

We use mullite as the first layer coating material because the coefficient of thermal expansion, which is $\sim 10^{-6}$ /K at room temperature, is close to that of alumina. Mullite ( $3{\rm Al}_{2}{\rm O}_{3}2{\rm SiO}_{2}$ ) is a silicate with a refractive index of 2.52. It is a porous ceramic material that can be applied to alumina using the thermal-spraying method offered by Tocalo Corporation [19]. This process uses an established and available technology and can be fabricated to a high precision of $10\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ in thickness. Mullite does not cause delamination under cryogenic conditions because it has a coefficient of thermal expansion matched that of alumina [12]. Mullite has a surface roughness due to its asperity structure. The design value of the thickness is $0.212\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ at MF and $0.097\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ at UHF based on X-ray CT and optical measurements.

### 3.4 Duroid

We use Duroid 5880LZ manufactured by Rogers Corporation as the second layer. Duroid 5880LZ is a matrix of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) loaded with a filler of $50\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ diameter hollow, nitrogen-filled, aluminosilicate microspheres with a refractive index of 1.41 at millimeter wave [20]. The manufactured thickness of the Duroid sheet is $500\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ , and we machine it down to 385 $\pm$ 10 µm for MF and 155 $\pm$ 10 µm for UHF at Suzuno Giken [36].

### 3.5 Epo-Tek

We use Epo-Tek 301-2, an aerosolized optical epoxy manufactured at Epoxy Technology [21] as a glue to apply the Duroid sheet to the mullite layer. We assume the refractive index of Epo-Tek is 1.7 at the millimeter wavelengths, which is between 1.53 at $600\text{\,}\mathrm{n}$ and 1.9 of the static value [31, 21]. The difference in reflectance due to these differences is less than 0.4%, which indicates that Epo-Tek does not compromise the optical performance. The thickness of the Epo-Tek layer is 40 µm (Figure 2).

## 4 Fabrication and quality control

### 4.1 Fabrication

Figure 3 shows the fabrication process. As a small test sample, a $105\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ square of alumina with a thickness of $4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ is used. In the process, we check the optical performance every time we add a layer to confirm the properties of each layer.

The first layer, mullite, is thermally sprayed on both alumina surfaces [12]. Atmospheric plasma spraying by Tocalo Corporation enables deposition with an accuracy of 10 µm [19]. The second layer of Duroid is glued on with 40 µm-thick Epo-Tek. To compute the accurate model during simulation, the reflectance is calculated with three layers, including the thin layer of Epo-Tek. Epo-Tek is applied to the Duroid side and uniformly bonded to the mullite. We first use a roller to remove the air bubbles from the bond interfaces, and then the assembly is vacuum bagged to apply a uniform load while curing the epoxy. After gluing, we dice the Duroid sheet to prevent peeling due to heat shrinkage using a box cutter into $40\times 40$ mm square islands for stress relief, while the mullite layer is not diced after applying the Duroid sheet. The cut widths are typically less than 100 µm, and no optical degradation is expected.

### 4.2 Quality control

The key to control quality is uniform and robust coatings. The Duroid sheets must be securely coated to the mullite surface to avoid air gaps, which would cause delamination in vacuum and cryogenic conditions. The fabricated coatings must be tested non-destructively. We developed three tests: an IR camera test, a tape peeling test, and a cryo-mechanical test. The IR camera test is crucial in establishing the fabrication process. Our testing found that all coatings that passed the IR camera test also successfully cleared the cryo-mechanical tests. In addition, optical characterization is essential to evaluate the optical performance of AR coatings. We will discuss the optical tests in Section 5.

We use an IR camera to look for areas of low thermal conductivity (i.e., areas with air gaps) to diagnose whether the adhesion is successful. The procedure is to warm the fabricated sample uniformly to $60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius}$ in a thermostatic chamber [39]. The surface is then photographed using an IR camera. Figure 4 shows the example of the IR view for both good and delaminated samples. If the sample is not well adhered, the surface will show cold spots, as shown in the right panel of Figure 4.

*Figure 4: Image of the Duroid surface using an Infrared camera for a good (left) and a failed (right) sample. The diameter is $505\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ . The delamination areas are observed as cold spots due to poor thermal conductivity.*

We employ a tape peeling test after the IR camera test. The surface of the coating is pulled using tape and checked to see if the adhesive strength is sufficient. We select a tape with appropriate adhesion properties because using too much adhesion could cause the surface to be torn. We use curing tape [40] as it does not damage the surface and has good consistency of results, as shown by the IR camera test.

We perform a cooldown test as a cryo-mechanical test to ensure the fabricated samples do not delaminate when cooled. We cool the large-diameter coatings more than two times to $30\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ . No delamination after the cooldown occurred for samples that had passed the IR and tape test.

### 4.3 Sapphire coating feasibility

It is challenging to coat directly on a sapphire surface. We can not apply the same approach to directly coat sapphire with mullite because sapphire is vulnerable to cracking during the required pre-heating step due to its internal stress. We can prevent this damage by annealing the sapphire, which relaxes the internal stress 11 1 The annealing process is performed by KYOCERA Cooperation [41].. The mullite coating process on annealed sapphire follows the same process applied to alumina. The systematic errors in the measurement are estimated using an alumina slab as a reference, for which the refractive index and thickness can be measured well. ### 5.2 Transmittance

We measure the transmission for some samples to estimate the AR coating’s loss tangent, $\tan\delta$ . One can reasonably expect that the loss properties of the material are rather stable between samples; we thus consider that transmission measurements of only a limited number of samples suffice for our needs. Absorption increases as the frequency increases, and it is necessary to estimate them, especially for the UHF samples with high absorption.

Figure 10 shows the schematics and setup of transmittance measurements for test samples. The measurement method is the same as that for reflectance measurements. The angle of incidence is zero degrees, but the sample is tilted about five degrees to reduce standing waves. The average transmittance of a 105 mm $\times$ 105 mm UHF sample (S2 in Table 2) is 85% for UHF1 and 80% for UHF2, respectively, at ambient temperature [43]. This transmittance can be considered a lower limit. The loss tangent is expected to decrease, and transmittance will increase at low temperatures.

*Figure 10: Left: Schematic of the transmittance measurement setup. The yellow lines indicate the optical path. The setup is almost the same as the reflection measurement. Right: Picture of the measurement setup for transmission. The sample is tilted a few degrees to avoid standing waves.*

We developed a setup to measure transmittance at cryogenic temperatures. The transmittance of a UHF sample is measured with the same VNA as the room temperature measurement. It is possible to take measurements quickly since they do not need a cryostat. There are two conditions for the measurement setup.

- • $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ condensation must not form in the optical path.

- • The measured sample must be cooled to about $100\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , below which we do not expect much difference in the loss tangent of coatings between $100\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ and 4, 40, or $80\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ .

Figure 11 shows the measurement setup. A box with Zotefoam (Plastazote HD30 [44]) is transparent to millimeter waves and nitrogen vapor cools the sample. There are two factors that prevent $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ condensation in the optical path. The first is that the flowing nitrogen vapor is saturated, preventing the air from taking in more water inside the box. The second is that the paths from the nitrogen vapor to the outside (airflow in Figure 11) are folded, and silicone rubber heaters SBH2117 [45] are placed in the middle of the paths to warm up the nitrogen vapor. This structure gives the nitrogen vapor enough time to warm up, ensuring that the box surface remains warm enough not to cool the outside air. To cool the sample sufficiently, we hold it with oxygen-free copper, which has high thermal conductivity. Copper surrounds the four sides of the sample, and the sample is cooled by thermal contact. To measure the transmittance accurately, two holders are prepared to side by side, one for holding the sample and the other for normalization without a sample. The transmission is first normalized by measuring a sample-free holder; then, the measurement point is shifted to the sample to measure transmittance. It eliminates the effects of copper edges, such as scattering. The validity of the measurement system and the check for water droplets are confirmed by measuring a $4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ alumina slab at 90–140 GHz.

## 6 Conclusion

We developed a two-layer AR coating for a sapphire HWP and an IR filter for CMB polarimetry at 90/150 and 220/280 GHz frequencies. The production process is established for cryogenic use and large diameters. We establish a quality control method. The coatings do not delaminate after a cooling cycle. The IR camera test enables quality assurance of the fabricated coatings. Our coatings with mullite and Duroid 5880LZ reduce the reflectivity to about 2.6%(0.9%). The transmittance is increased to about 90% in actual use, as evaluated at cryogenic temperature. Such a production process for coating large optical surfaces is essential for modern CMB experiments. The HWPs and IR filters with our coating are used in the Simons Array and the Simons Observatory experiments. They are installed in the receiver at the site. This technique will also be applied to optical elements for future CMB experiments, such as CMB-S4.

## 1  Introduction

POLARBEAR-2b (PB-2b) is the second receiver in the Simons Array, a cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization experiment [1]. PB-2b was installed on its telescope in 2022 in the Atacama Desert at an altitude of 5.2 km. The telescope has a 3.5 m primary and detectors with arcminute resolution. Of the 7500 detectors, 2072 have so far been calibrated with planet observations. The readout system used is digital frequency multiplexing electronics (DfMUX) [2]. This paper will cover early results from the commissioning of the readout electronics, focusing of the optics, and preliminary tests of bolometer performance.

Ambient temperature electronics amplify the signal further, filter the output to minimize aliasing, and digitize the signal [3]. Since the installation of the receiver, about 75% of the DfMUX readout electronics have been commissioned. ## 3  Bolometer Performance

Bolometer performance is being evaluated and their operation optimized. In addition to estimating the noise equivalent temperature of a detector from planet observations, we are using a new method to monitor the loopgain of detectors in the transition. Received: 2 November 2023 / Accepted: 22 April 2024 / Published online: 26 May 2024 © The Author(s) 2024

Abstract Cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments have deployed focal planes with O(104) transition edge sensor (TES) bolometers cooled to sub-Kelvin temperatures by multiplexing the readout of many TES channels onto a single pair of wires. Digital Frequency-domain Multiplexing (DfMux) is a multiplexing technique used in many CMB polarization experiments, such as the Simons Array, SPT-3 G, and EBEX. The DfMux system studied here uses LC filters with resonant frequencies ranging from 1.5 to 4.5 MHz connected to an array of TESs. Each detector has an amplitude-modulated carrier tone at the resonant frequency of its accompanying LC resonator. The signal is recovered via quadrature demodulation where the in-phase (I) component of the demodulated current is in phase with the complex admittance of the circuit and the quadrature (Q) component is orthogonal to I. Observed excess current noise in the Q component is consistent with fluctuations in the resonant frequency. This noise has been shown to be non-orthogonal to the phase of the detector’s responsivity. We present a detailed analysis of the phase of responsivity of the TES and noise sources in our DfMux readout system. Further, we investigate how modifications to the TES operating resistance and bias frequency can affect the phase of noise relative to the phase of the detector responsivity, using data from Simons Array to evaluate our predictions. We find that both the phase of responsivity and phase of noise are functions of the two tuning parameters, which can be purposefully selected to maximize signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio.

## 1  Introduction

Simons Array (SA) is an experiment located in the Atacama Desert in Chile at an altitude of 5200 m. The goal of Simons Array is to measure the polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background using O(104) transition-edge sensor (TES) bolometers in its two receivers, PB-2a and PB-2b [1, 2]. To read out its thousands of detectors, Simons Array utilizes digital frequencydomain multiplexing (DfMux) with a multiplexing factor of 40× . In this scheme, each TES detector is assigned a frequency channel by being connected in series with an inductor and capacitor (LC) resonator. The TES resistance, inductor and capacitor form an LCR “leg” with resonant frequency fr , and each TES is voltage biased by a carrier containing independent tones at the different fr . As the optical power on the TES changes, its resistance changes and results in an amplitude modulation of the current through each leg. The signal from the TESs is amplified first by a Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) Array Amplifier (SAA), and then by room temperature electronics before being demodulated. The singlestage SAAs are of the NIST SA13a design, which was selected for Simons Array after its characterization reported in [3]. The 210 SAAs are located in the 4 K stage to limit the thermal load onto the sub-Kelvin stages. To linearize the SAA output and maximize dynamic range, current through the SAA is nulled using the technique of Digital Active Nulling (DAN)[4]. The nulling of currents at the SAA junction also has the benefit of suppressing the SAA input inductance in DAN’s effective circuit admittance. A simplified circuit of the readout scheme is shown in Fig. 1, where some parasitic components are included. Two-level states in the LC resonator chips of Simons Array were found to induce phase noise [5]. While the phase noise was initially expected to not have a significant impact on the SNR of SA detectors, its actual contribution hadn’t yet been quantified.

2.1  How Phase is Defined in DfMux

When the current signal gets demodulated by room temperature electronics, it is decomposed using I/Q demodulation. The I (in-phase) component is aligned to the phase of the carrier ∠Icarrier and by consequence to the phase of admittance ∠Y , where Y = Icarrier∕Vb and Vb is the voltage bias. The phase of the demodulation is chosen to be anti-aligned with the phase of the nuller signal to ensure cancellation at the SQUID summing junction. Every time that the carrier current is adjusted to either bring the TES into, or out of, their superconducting transitions, the phase of the carrier is adjusted to ensure that < Q >= 0.

2.3  Phases of Noise

The major sources of noise in PB-2a (photon, phonon, readout and Johnson noise) can be decomposed according to their associated phases. Photon noise and phonon noise are power sources on the TES, which are converted to current noises via the detector responsivity. Thus, by definition, these noise sources only contribute to the total noise in-phase with responsivity. Broadband readout noise has no preferential phase and thus generates equal contributions in and out of phase with the TES responsivity. This is the case for SQUID noise and noise from room temperature electronics. There are three noise sources that are expected to be mostly out of phase with responsivity. First, TES Johnson noise is suppressed by the detector’s electrothermal feedback. However, by definition, this suppression does not occur out-of-phase with responsivity [8]. Second, as described in [7], leakage current and power crosstalk from neighboring TESs are expected to be many degrees out-of-phase with the signal phase. Finally, two-level system noise has been seen in lithographed superconducting resonator chips, and is caused by the coupling of the resonator to a thin amorphous solid dielectric layer where two-level tunneling states are thought to exist [9]. This noise is equivalent to a jitter in the resonance frequency, which has manifested itself as an excess noise in the Q component of the current in SA hardware utilizing DfMux [5]. It is important for experiments using DfMux that the excess phase noise does not increase noise in the responsivity phase of the detectors. We’ve added to the characterization of noise from [5] by investigating the impact of detector operating resistance Rfrac and bias frequency onto the phase that minimizes noise. As part of this study, we’ve measured instrument noise when the TES is biased ±450 Hz off from the LC resonance peak. This induces additional reactances to the readout circuit which cause shifts to the phase of responsivity. This effect can be utilized in an attempt to best align the phase of detector responsivity with the phase that minimizes the noise in the demodulated signal. In addition, the added impedance can increase TES responsivity [10], increasing the overall SNR. Similarly to how the phase of responsivity is measured in SA TESs, we measure the phase of minimum noise by recursive offline phase rotations until the median of the I′ ASD between 6 and 9 Hz has been minimized. This frequency range is chosen to avoid resonances from the stimulator signal at 5 Hz while still capturing noise within the detector’s time response.1

As detectors go lower into their superconducting transition, their responsivity phases start to spread further, as shown in the left panel of Fig. 2. This is expected as the reactances in the circuit induce higher phase shifts when the TES resistance is smaller, as suggested by Eq. 2. An example of the model predicted phase shifts relative to the demodulation phase compared to the measured ones can be seen on the right panel of Fig. 2. The data is from TESs from three separate LC circuits currently in the PB-2a receiver. These three circuits were chosen due to their associated lower Chi-squared in the fit of the measured impedance to the model of Fig. 1, which resulted in better agreement with the responsivity phase predictions. In other words, accurate modelling of the readout impedances allows us to predict the phase response of our detectors, which is not necessarily aligned with I.

3.2  Offset Between Phase of Responsivity and Phase of Noise

When detectors are saturated and not in transition, we see a larger noise amplitude in the Q component of the demodulated current than in the I component, as shown in the top left panel of Fig. 3. In this state, the phase of minimum noise would be aligned with I. However, when detectors are in transition, more factors can affect the phase of dominant noise. As discussed in the previous section, the responsivity is not necessarily aligned with I. In addition, when detectors are in transition, noise sources aligned with responsivity contribute to the noise budget. Furthermore, the decreased TES resistance can change the impact of the phase shifts induced by circuit parasitic impedances on the noise.

3.3  Off‑Resonance Biasing

Biasing away from the resonance that maximizes the admittance described in 2.2 will further shift the phase of responsivity from the phase of circuit impedance. The left panel of Fig. 4 shows the responsivity phase shift for many different SA TESs, whereas the right panel shows an example of a single TES’s phases of maximum signal and of minimum noise at different bias frequencies. The point of intersection between the two lines shows where the offset between those two phases can be minimized by optimizing the bias frequency, indicating that biasing detectors slightly off-resonance is a strategy that can be used to align maximum signal and minimum noise phases in SA TESs.

4  Conclusion

We investigated the responsivity and noise phase behavior in the DfMux scheme implemented in the Simons Array’s PB-2a receiver. Both phases were found to depend on TES tuning parameters such as Rfrac and bias frequencies, and we were able to predict the responsivity phase behavior by characterizing the impedances in the cold readout. Adding a small offset to the detectors’ bias frequency resulted in shifting both responsivity and noise phases. This effect could be used to align phase of maximum responsivity and phase of minimum noise.
